11	## Prose form
12	
13	([why](rationale.md#prose-form))
14	
15	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why* or
16	the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
17	[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
18	numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One fact
19	per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they
20	hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their
21	relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See [Semicolons](#semicolons) and [Typeable
22	punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
23	
24	Surfaces that use this shape:
25	
26	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See [Doc
27	  comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
28	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and agent-repo). The title is the commit-specific add-on.
29	  See [The per-rung flow](../AGENTS.md#the-per-rung-flow).
30	- The cycle-record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`. See [The In Progress
31	  block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).
32	- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are
33	  still fine.
34	
35	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
36	
37	- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged by
38	  [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
39	  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader meets
40	    first and it answers the problem
41	  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them is
42	    a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
43	  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A bullet
44	    wanting a paragraph belongs in the cycle-record instead
45	  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
46	    live in the cycle-record, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names, each
47	    reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs here
48	- **Cycle-record / todo**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what landed
49	  and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list. The diff
50	  is the mechanical record, the commit body the problem and solution, the cycle-record the design
51	  thinking, and none restates another.
52	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
53	
54	### Leads are labels, unmarked
55	
56	In a list item or a numbered step, a lead is a short label ending in a colon, with no markup, and
57	the sentence after it is complete without it:
58	
59	```
60	1. Backfill: fill every as-built ladder whose commits have landed, before anything else.
61	```
62	
63	- Label names, sentence instructs: a reader's eye takes bold at the head of an item as the item's
64	  name and resumes at the plain text expecting a full sentence, so a bold lead that is the
65	  sentence's own verb or subject (`**Backfill** every as-built ladder ...`) loses its imperative to
66	  the reader who skips it. Measured 2026-08-21, at the review of the rule that example is from: the
67	  reviewer read "every as-built ladder" and stopped, with nothing telling them what to do.
68	- The inverted case: a rule stated in bold is the same failure inverted. When the bold is a whole
69	  sentence and the plain text is commentary, the reader who skips bold reads the commentary as the
70	  rule. The fix is the same: a short name as the label, the rule as the plain sentence. The hard
71	  rules in AGENTS.md are the instance, and the names they gained are greppable and survive a
72	  renumbering.
73	- Definitions: the same shape, `Term: what it means.` A period after a bold term (`**Term.** ...`)
74	  reads as a heading, which is the label reading again.
75	- No markup on the label: bold is what makes the eye treat the lead as a heading and skip it, and
76	  the agent-files are read by an agent, which needs no emphasis. The colon alone marks the label
77	  (wink, 2026-08-21).
78	- The price: one word of redundancy, paid on purpose: the label is skippable, the sentence is not.
79	
80	### One spelling per term
81	
82	A defined term has one spelling, everywhere: `work-repo` and `agent-repo` are always hyphenated,
83	`agent-files`, `version-of-record`, `dual-repo`, and `as-built` likewise, and no rule varies the
84	spelling by how the term is used. Terminology in AGENTS.md defines the terms, and this section is
85	where the spelling rule lives, since a glossary is read for meaning rather than for spelling.
86	
87	### Bullet form
88	
89	A bullet is a full sentence, capitalized and ending in a period or question mark, unless the list
90	is a plain list of things (files, names, options), which takes neither. A list is all one or all
91	the other. A sentence never opens with a lower-case name (`squash-push`, `rationale.md`), it is
92	recast so the name is not the first word.
93	
94	### Line widths
95	
96	Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather than
97	restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated 2026-08-09,
98	when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.
99	
100	- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
101	- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
102	  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
103	- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
104	- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
105	  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.
106	
107	The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps when
108	touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than imitating the
109	narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL, a literal report
110	row, indented code in a comment).
111	
112	### Problem-first shape
113	
114	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper form of the same
115	shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.
116	
117	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate what
118	  follows it.
119	- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms, answering
120	  whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in [Bullet content
121	  differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
122	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
123	  - In Progress: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See [Conventional-commit
124	    shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) for the per-step title + `(current)` /
125	    `(done)` form.
126	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is picked up
127	    into a cycle.
128	
129	**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A cycle
130	writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's commit
131	body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a commit body's
132	is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule here said a plan
133	was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle unable to say at its
134	opening what it intended to do.
135

[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One fact
per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they
hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their
relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See [Semicolons](#semicolons) and [Typeable
punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See [Doc
  comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and agent-repo). The title is the commit-specific add-on.
  See [The per-rung flow](../AGENTS.md#the-per-rung-flow).
- The cycle-record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`. See [The In Progress
  block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).
- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are
  still fine.

Bullet *content* differs by surface:

- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged by
  [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader meets
    first and it answers the problem
  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them is
    a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A bullet
    wanting a paragraph belongs in the cycle-record instead
  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
    live in the cycle-record, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names, each
    reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs here
- **Cycle-record / todo**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what landed
  and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list. The diff
  is the mechanical record, the commit body the problem and solution, the cycle-record the design
  thinking, and none restates another.
- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).

### Leads are labels, unmarked

In a list item or a numbered step, a lead is a short label ending in a colon, with no markup, and
the sentence after it is complete without it:

```
1. Backfill: fill every as-built ladder whose commits have landed, before anything else.
```

- Label names, sentence instructs: a reader's eye takes bold at the head of an item as the item's
  name and resumes at the plain text expecting a full sentence, so a bold lead that is the
  sentence's own verb or subject (`**Backfill** every as-built ladder ...`) loses its imperative to
  the reader who skips it. Measured 2026-08-21, at the review of the rule that example is from: the
  reviewer read "every as-built ladder" and stopped, with nothing telling them what to do.
- The inverted case: a rule stated in bold is the same failure inverted. When the bold is a whole
  sentence and the plain text is commentary, the reader who skips bold reads the commentary as the
  rule. The fix is the same: a short name as the label, the rule as the plain sentence. The hard
  rules in AGENTS.md are the instance, and the names they gained are greppable and survive a
  renumbering.
- Definitions: the same shape, `Term: what it means.` A period after a bold term (`**Term.** ...`)
  reads as a heading, which is the label reading again.
- No markup on the label: bold is what makes the eye treat the lead as a heading and skip it, and
  the agent-files are read by an agent, which needs no emphasis. The colon alone marks the label
  (wink, 2026-08-21).
- The price: one word of redundancy, paid on purpose: the label is skippable, the sentence is not.

### One spelling per term

A defined term has one spelling, everywhere: `work-repo` and `agent-repo` are always hyphenated,
`agent-files`, `version-of-record`, `dual-repo`, and `as-built` likewise, and no rule varies the
spelling by how the term is used. Terminology in AGENTS.md defines the terms, and this section is
where the spelling rule lives, since a glossary is read for meaning rather than for spelling.

### Bullet form

A bullet is a full sentence, capitalized and ending in a period or question mark, unless the list
is a plain list of things (files, names, options), which takes neither. A list is all one or all
the other. A sentence never opens with a lower-case name (`squash-push`, `rationale.md`), it is
recast so the name is not the first word.

### Line widths

Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather than
restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated 2026-08-09,
when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.

- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.

The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps when
touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than imitating the
narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL, a literal report
row, indented code in a comment).

### Problem-first shape

`## In Progress` cycle blocks, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper form of the same
shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.

- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate what
  follows it.
- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms, answering
  whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in [Bullet content
  differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
  - In Progress: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See [Conventional-commit
    shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) for the per-step title + `(current)` /
    `(done)` form.
  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is picked up
    into a cycle.

**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A cycle
writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's commit
body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a commit body's
is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule here said a plan
was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle unable to say at its
opening what it intended to do.

input.new_string:
### A setup-host command, the pin profiles first

The template's `[profiles]` are a 3900X's, `smt = "0,12"`, `ccx = "0,1"`, `ccd = "0,6"`, so a
fresh config on any other host starts from cpu numbers that are wrong there, and on this one from
the busy end (wink, 2026-09-19). `setup-freq` already answers the same problem for `[freq]`, the
live host read and its table written to the XDG file, and nothing does it for the rest.

A `setup-host` command writes every table that is the host's own, `[profiles]` first, with
`setup-freq` becoming its `[freq]` part. It follows [Placements by name and a cpus
command](#placements-by-name-and-a-cpus-command), whose rule picks the cpus.

- The facts are already probed: `host.rs` reads each cache index's `shared_cpus`, L1's naming the
  SMT siblings and L3's the CCX, so the pairs are derived and `lscpu -e` is no longer the advice.
- The cpus come from the placements rule, the base the last core's primary cpu, never from a rule
  of this entry's own, so a written profile and a built-in name land on the same pair: `11,23`,
  `11,10`, and `11,8` on the 3900X.
- The open question is what a written `[profiles]` is for once `smt`, `ccx`, and `x-ccx` resolve
  built-in. We think it is the rule's answer made visible and editable, a pool of four or a
  base other than the default, and that a host whose file has none loses nothing.
- A profile the host cannot form is left out with a comment saying why, `x-ccx` on the 7600X's
  one L3, never written with a wrong pair. The kernel does not expose the CCD on AM4, so `ccd`
  goes and `x-ccx` is what can be derived.
- The output follows `init-config`'s rule, TOML without the prose when the XDG file is
  `config.toml` and the markdown form otherwise, creating a missing file, appending a missing
  table, and leaving a declared one alone, as `setup-freq` does.
- The config's values are of three kinds, and only the first is this entry's: a host fact that
  can be read (`[freq]`, `[profiles]`), a host value that must be measured (`pin_mhz`,
  `settle_time`, `warm_cap`, `blocks`, `duration`, `runs`), and a default that is the same
  everywhere (`decimals`, `band_labels`, `trim_runs`). The measured kind is a calibration
  command, what `feat: a shorter trustworthy run on the 7600x` works out by hand, and is an
  entry of its own once that cycle says what to measure first.

### init-config prints TOML when asked

A bare `init-config` prints the markdown form whatever becomes of it, so `init-config > x.toml`
writes 221 lines of prose into a `.toml` name, a file the loader refuses, where
`init-config x.toml` writes the 60-line TOML form (wink, 2026-09-19, at
`config-iiac-perf-7600x-default.toml`). The form follows PATH's extension and the standard
output has none.

- We think the answer is a flag that names the form, `--format toml`, for the standard output
  alone, PATH's extension still deciding a written file, decided at the opening.
- What `update-config` writes is unchanged, the form of the file it rewrites.

by hand. A `figures RECORDS OUT_DIR` subcommand draws the write-up's SVGs on `series.rs`'s
arithmetic, a subcommand because the crate is one binary and an example could not reach its

##### docs: the overhead floor on the 7600x

About 4 s of every 7.2 s run is overhead, and `d*` goes as its square root, so it is cut first.
`settle_time` and `run_sleep` binary-search down, monotone; `block_sleep` and `block_warmup` get a
three-point comparison instead, since a sleep of zero collapses the blocks into one continuous run
and a sleep provokes the ramp the warmup exists to discard, so neither is monotone in stability.

checks the measured `CI95 runs` against what the model predicts, so the model is calibrated rather
than trusted.

five sessions and the `min-now` confirmation, ships the config, and writes what each knob bought

The `init-config` entry in `TODO.md` now carries your decision. A redirected standard output gets TOML, a terminal still gets the markdown form, and `--format md|toml` overrides both. One point is marked "We think" for the opening to decide: a flag that contradicts the path's extension should be an error, so a file's name never lies about its contents.

On recording runs for `analyze` from a config: yes. Here is what I would settle before recording.

**Existing data and what new data adds.**
- The rung's text says its tests reproduce "the baseline's numbers from the tracked records".
  - `records/knobs.jsonl` already holds them: three conditions of eight invocations of ten runs of `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` on the 7600X, plus a 100-run series.
  - The records keep each run's mean, so the lower-band trim recomputes from them.
- That data is one bench at the old 7.2 s settings, and we think it never fails calibration.
- Today's pair of invocations showed the failure `analyze` exists to catch. `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` sits on two levels, and its `LSC trimmed` missed by 42x.
- So new data earns its place by bringing a bench that breaks the claim and the short settings, not by adding more of the same.

**The config I would write.**
- Benches: three, not `all`.
  - `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` is the cycle's subject, `min-now` is its confirmation, and `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` is the known failure.
  - A record is about 4.3 KB, so `all` at 20 invocations is about 24 MB, too big to track. Three benches come to about 2.6 MB, the size of `knobs.jsonl`.
- Settings: today's short ones.
  - They are `duration = 0.25`, `runs = 10`, `blocks = 10`, `run_sleep = "100ms"`, `settle_time = 0.1`, `warm_cap = 0.1`, `block_sleep = "100-200ms"` and `pin_freq = "pin_mhz"`.
  - They are not yet justified, which is the later rungs' job. That is fine here: `analyze` is what will judge them.
- Record: `record = "records/claim.jsonl"` with a `[tags]` entry `experiment = "claim"`.
  - This gives one file per experiment, as the deliberation settled.
  - Today's `./tmp/` directory form is right for scratch and wrong for data the tests will read.
- Pinning: `pin_cpus = "smt"`, a profile name instead of cpu numbers.
  - A named config takes `[profiles]` from the host's XDG file.
  - So one unedited file runs on both hosts if each XDG file declares `smt` by hand today: `"11,23"` on the 3900X and `"5,11"` on the 7600X.
  - This is the payoff of the profiles discussion, available now with no code.

**What the config cannot hold.**
- Repetition is a shell loop around the run, since no key repeats invocations. The loop line goes in the config's leading comment so the experiment is reproducible from the file alone.
- The host is not touched while it runs.
  - At about 2.1 s per run, three benches of ten runs take about 63 s per invocation.
  - Twenty invocations take about 21 minutes. Compute that, wait, and look once.

The plain version: write one small config with three benches, one of them known to fool the error bar. Run it twenty times in a loop on each host without touching the machine, and keep the result as test data. Pin by the name `smt` so the same file works on both hosts.

- May I add `[profiles]` with `smt = "11,23"` to this host's `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md`? You would add `smt = "5,11"` on the 7600X.

content.text:
`configs/claim.toml` is written and both `config-iiac-perf-7600x-*` files are fixed; all three parse. The `[profiles]` edit to your XDG config did not happen: the sandbox makes `~/.config/iiac-perf/` read-only (`Read-only file system`), so that one is yours to do.

**`configs/claim.toml`**
- I generated it with `init-config --from /dev/null` from the run line, so it is the standard TOML form.
- It sets the three benches and today's short settings:

```toml
benches = ["zcr-spsc-v3-2t", "min-now", "zcr-spsc-v3-1t"]
duration = 0.25
settle_time = 0.1
warm_cap = 0.1
runs = 10
run_sleep = "100ms"
blocks = 10
block_sleep = "100-200ms"
block_warmup = "2ms"
pin_cpus = "smt"
record = "records/claim.jsonl"
pin_freq = "pin_mhz"

[tags]
experiment = "claim"
```

- Its header comment covers these points:
  - What the experiment asks.
  - Why `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` is included.
  - That the host is not touched while it runs.
  - Where `smt` has to be declared.
  - The loop line, which is below.

```
for i in $(seq 20); do iiac-perf configs/claim.toml; done
```

**The two 7600x files**
- When I came to fix `config-iiac-perf-7600x-default.toml` it was no longer the markdown file. You had already rewritten it into the TOML form.
- What was wrong in both files was the copied `[freq]` table with this 3900X's clamp (1745 to 4673, pin 3801).
- It got there because both were made with `--from iiac-perf.md`.
  - `--from` carries the old file's own values, and the repo's `iiac-perf.md` declares `[freq]`.
  - I checked `update-config` and a bare `init-config`: neither copies it.
- I put `#[freq]` back in both.
  - The default file now sets only `blocks = 100`, `block_sleep = "1-10ms"`, `block_warmup = "2ms"`.
  - The `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` file keeps its run keys, `pin_cpus = "5,11"` and its tag.
- I left `pin_cpus = "5,11"` as numbers in the `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` file, since it is named for one host. Say so if you want `"smt"` there too.
- The tracked `iiac-perf.md` still carries this host's `[freq]`. A checkout on the 7600X would get the 3900X's clamp from it, and any `--from iiac-perf.md` will copy it again.
  - We think that table belongs only in each host's XDG file.
  - I did not touch it.

**Still to do**
- Append this to `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md` here, and the same on the 7600X with `smt = "5,11"`:

````markdown
```toml
[profiles]
smt = "11,23"
```
````

- Until then `configs/claim.toml` will not run: `smt` is not a profile yet, so it would be read as a cpu spec and rejected.
- I have not run the experiment. It is about 21 minutes of a host nobody touches, so it is yours to start. If you run it from this session, I will wait out the computed time and look once, as the deliberation says.
- The working copy now holds `TODO.md`, `configs/claim.toml`, the two fixed configs, and `smooth-3900x-all-run.md`. These all go into the next `vc-x1 push` unless moved first.

- **References I left alone:**

The comment is deleted. `iiac-perf.toml` now sets `blocks = 100`, `block_sleep = "1-10ms"` and `block_warmup = "2ms"` with no rationale above them.

You were right to doubt it. The cycle's own Problem statement says "the block knee sits near 16 of the 100 blocks", so "a hundred blocks ... the size the grades were tuned on" is a claim this cycle is already taking apart.

**Your reading of `smooth-3900x-all-run.md`.**
- It is half right, and the half matters.
- Precision is there. On the last core's SMT pair at 0.25 s a run, 20 of 28 benches repeated their trimmed mean within 0.5% a day apart, and 16 within 0.12%. On this host unpinned, the block means had a lag-1 autocorrelation of +0.78.
- Calibration is not there. 7 of 28 benches moved more than their `LSC trimmed` claimed, and `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` moved 42 times more.
- By the cycle's own definition, "precision and calibration, not precision alone", those settings are a strong candidate and not yet trustworthy.
- `smt` is also not a neutral "quiet cpus" choice for the two-thread benches. The template itself calls it "the most contention" and calls `ccx` "the best channel latency".
  - A `zcr-*-2t` number on `11,23` measures a ring across two siblings sharing an L1 and L2, a different thing from `11,10`.
  - The pair is quiet because it is the last core. `ccx = "11,10"` is on that core too, so we think it would be equally quiet.
  - So which profile `iiac-perf.toml` names is a decision about what the repo's default number means, separate from how smooth it is.

**The goal and where it belongs.**
- I agree with the goal, and it is better than the cycle's current one.
  - The acceptance check ships `configs/quick.toml`, a file someone has to know to ask for.
  - `iiac-perf.toml` is what every bare run in this repo gets.
  - Making the project-local file the example of "quick and trustworthy" means the default is the finding.
- I would not make it the goal of the `analyze` rung.
  - That rung builds the tool that judges a config.
  - Writing the candidate into `iiac-perf.toml` there would call it trustworthy before anything has checked it. The deliberation already covers this: "A candidate is not a finding until it survives repetition."
- The order I would keep is:
  - `configs/claim.toml` is the candidate under test, and its twenty invocations are the first evidence.
  - `analyze` reads them and says which benches back their claim.
  - The `docs: the overhead floor on the 7600x` and `docs: the run length at the new overhead` rungs say whether 0.25 s and ten blocks are the right values or merely lucky ones.
  - The `feat: the quick config for the 7600x` rung then writes the surviving values into `iiac-perf.toml` instead of `configs/quick.toml`, and puts the true comment above them.
- So the change to the cycle is small:
  - Retarget the last work rung and the acceptance check from `configs/quick.toml` to `iiac-perf.toml`.
  - Add a deliberation bullet with your name and today's date.
  - Nothing pushed gets renamed.

**What I need from you.**
- The cycle is titled "on the 7600x" and its deliberation says "The 7600X alone", with the 3900X as the Todo `### A shorter run on the 3900X, and the allocation hint`. But `iiac-perf.toml` is one file for both hosts.
- Which do you want?
  - Keep the 7600X as the acceptance host, with the 3900X claim data riding along as evidence. This is my lean, because it keeps the scope.
  - Widen this cycle's check to both hosts.
- Once the file pins by profile name, every bare run in the repo needs the host's XDG file to declare that name, or the run fails. That is acceptable, and `setup-host` later removes the friction, but the rung should say so.
- Which profile becomes the default, `smt` or `ccx`? I lean `ccx` for the default. `smt` measures the contended case and stays one flag away.

The plain version: the short settings look precise on this machine but have not yet shown that their error bars can be believed. So `iiac-perf.toml` should get those values at the end of the cycle, once the repeated runs and the new `analyze` command say they hold. I'd change the cycle's final target from a separate `quick.toml` to `iiac-perf.toml` itself.

If you agree, I'll make the `TODO.md` edits. That is a change to the agreed plan, so it needs your go first.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# The pins experiment: what the cpu pin and the clock pin each buy, on this host.
#
# Six conditions, the cpu pin (hi, lo, none) crossed with the clock pin (pin, free), each an
# invocation of configs/pins.toml with its pins on the line and a tag for each factor. The
# conditions go round-robin, the start rotating each round, so a drift over the hour lands on
# every condition alike and none always follows the same neighbor. Run from the repo root, and
# leave the host alone until it ends: 8 rounds of 6 is 48 invocations, about 50 minutes.
#
#   configs/pins.sh HI LO [ROUNDS]
#   configs/pins.sh 11,23 0,12      # 3900X: the last core's SMT pair against the first's
#   configs/pins.sh 5,11 0,6        # 7600X
#
# BIN names the binary, iiac-perf-dev while a cycle runs.
set -euo pipefail

hi=${1:?HI cpus, as 11,23}
lo=${2:?LO cpus, as 0,12}
rounds=${3:-8}
bin=${BIN:-iiac-perf-dev}

conditions=("hi pin" "hi free" "lo pin" "lo free" "none pin" "none free")
n=${#conditions[@]}

for ((r = 0; r < rounds; r++)); do
    for ((i = 0; i < n; i++)); do
        read -r cpus freq <<<"${conditions[(r + i) % n]}"
        args=(configs/pins.toml --tag "cpus=$cpus" --tag "freq=$freq")
        case $cpus in
        hi) args+=(--pin-cpus "$hi") ;;
        lo) args+=(--pin-cpus "$lo") ;;
        esac
        if [[ $freq == pin ]]; then
            args+=(--pin-freq)
        fi
        echo "== round $((r + 1))/$rounds: cpus=$cpus freq=$freq"
        "$bin" "${args[@]}"
    done
done

content.text:
I wrote the experiment as `configs/pins.toml` plus `configs/pins.sh`. Running it has to be yours, because the sandbox can't pin the clock: my smoke test of `--pin-freq` failed with `writing "0" to /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cpufreq/boost: Read-only file system`.

**The design.** Your three hypotheses are two factors, so I cross them into six conditions.

| | clock pinned | clock free |
|---|---|---|
| upper cpus `11,23` | hi, pin | hi, free |
| lower cpus `0,12` | lo, pin | lo, free |
| unpinned | none, pin | none, free |

- "Upper cpus give good results even on the 3900X" is the `hi` row against the `lo` row.
  - `lo` is there because without it a good `hi` result can't be told apart from pinning in general.
- "Unpinned is still poor" is the `none` row against the other two.
- "`--pin-freq` always helps" is the left column against the right, in all three rows. The word "always" is the test: it has to win in every row, not only on average.

**The files.**
- `configs/pins.toml` holds the same three benches and short settings as `configs/claim.toml`, with no pin keys. It records to `records/pins.jsonl` with `experiment = "pins"`.
- `configs/pins.sh HI LO [ROUNDS]` runs the six conditions and adds `--pin-cpus`, `--pin-freq`, and two tags per invocation on the line: `cpus=hi|lo|none` and `freq=pin|free`. One tag per factor lets `analyze` group on either.
- The conditions go round-robin, not in blocks of eight.
  - An hour's drift in temperature or background load would otherwise land on whichever condition ran last.
  - The starting condition also rotates each round, so no condition always follows a clock restore.
- The script uses cpu numbers, not the `smt` profile, so it doesn't wait on the host config install.
  - `--pin-freq` needs the `[freq]` table in the host config, which is where it now lives.

**To run it**, from the repo root, then leave the host alone:

```
configs/pins.sh 11,23 0,12
```

- Eight rounds of six is 48 invocations of about 63 s, so about 50 minutes.
- Today's earlier run had 22 disturbed blocks in its first two minutes and none after, so walking away matters.

**What I expect, written down before the data.**
- `hi` beats `lo`. The placements Todo counts ten times the timer ticks on the first CCX.
- `none` is worst. The deliberation's lag-1 of +0.78 unpinned is the evidence so far.
- I am least sure of `--pin-freq`.
  - The clock pin should remove the drift between invocations.
  - We think it helps the unpinned row most and the `hi` row least, which would make "always" true but uneven.
- `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` fails calibration in every condition, because its two levels come from memory placement, not from cpus or the clock.
  - If a pin fixes it, that is a finding about what sets the level.

**What "good" will mean.** Per condition and bench I'll compare three things:
- the spread of the eight trimmed means;
- the average `LSC trimmed` they claimed;
- the ratio of the two.

The first two measure precision and the ratio measures calibration.

**Limits to keep in mind.**
- Eight invocations estimate a spread only to about plus or minus 50%. A threefold difference between conditions will show, and a 20% one will not. Pass `16` as the third argument if you want a finer answer; that doubles the time.
- `records/pins.jsonl` will be about 6 MB. We can decide whether to track it or keep it in `tmp/` when we see what it says.
- These are the short settings, so a poor result for a condition is poor at 0.25 s and ten blocks, not in general.

**Checks so far.**
- The script parses.
- An unpinned smoke run showed `bench pin none (unpinned)` and `tags cpus=none, experiment=pins, freq=free`.
- I have not run `vc-x1 validate` since adding these files.

The plain version: run the three benches under six combinations of where the threads sit and whether the clock is locked, eight times each, taking turns so time of day can't favour one. Then see which combinations repeat their own numbers and which don't. It takes about fifty minutes of an untouched machine.

Once it finishes, tell me and I'll read `records/pins.jsonl`. This also pushes the cycle-plan changes from my last message a bit further out, which I think is right: this data should inform them.

- Today's recorded run covers the same command with full data, and the comparison I drew from the capture is already made.

- So it is yours to start. Run this in your own terminal from the repo root, then leave the host alone for about 50 minutes:

cat > tmp/pins.py <<'EOF'
import json,statistics as st,math
from collections import defaultdict
T975={3:3.182}
inv=defaultdict(list)   # (bench,cpus,freq,series)->run means
blk=defaultdict(list)
for l in open('records/pins.jsonl'):
    try: r=json.loads(l)
    except Exception: continue
    k=(r['bench'],r['tags']['cpus'],r['tags']['freq'],r['series'])
    inv[k].append(r['mean_ns'])
    x=r['block_mean_ns']; m=sum(x)/len(x); d=sum((a-m)**2 for a in x)
    if d>0: blk[k[:3]].append(sum((x[i]-m)*(x[i+1]-m) for i in range(len(x)-1))/d)
def trimmed(v):
    s=sorted(v); k=s[1:5]; tm=sum(k)/4
    w=[s[1]]*2+s[1:5]+[s[4]]*0   # winsorize: ends replaced by kept edges over the 10-50 band
    return tm,k
cell=defaultdict(list)
for (b,c,f,s),v in inv.items():
    assert len(v)==10
    tm,k=trimmed(v)
    cell[(b,c,f)].append((tm,st.mean(v),max(k)-min(k),st.stdev(v)))
print(f"{'bench':16}{'cpus':5}{'freq':5}{'trim.mean':>10}{'sd(trim)%':>10}{'range%':>8}{'sd(plain)%':>11}{'kept-range%':>12}{'run sd%':>8}{'lag1':>6}")
for b in ['min-now','zcr-spsc-v3-1t','zcr-spsc-v3-2t']:
    for c in ['hi','lo','none']:
        for f in ['pin','free']:
            v=cell[(b,c,f)]; t=[x[0] for x in v]; p=[x[1] for x in v]
            g=st.mean(t)
            print(f"{b:16}{c:5}{f:5}{g:10.3f}{st.stdev(t)/g*100:10.3f}{(max(t)-min(t))/g*100:8.2f}{st.stdev(p)/st.mean(p)*100:11.2f}{st.mean(x[2] for x in v)/g*100:12.3f}{st.mean(x[3] for x in v)/g*100:8.2f}{st.mean(blk[(b,c,f)]):6.2f}")
    print()
EOF

content.text:
The experiment completed: 48 invocations, 80 records in each of the 18 cells, and no errors. `records/pins.jsonl` is 7.2 MB.

Your first hypothesis holds but not for the reason you gave, the second holds for two-thread benches only, and the third is wrong as worded, though the clock pin buys something else.

The main table is spread across each condition's eight trimmed means, as a percent of the mean:

| bench | cpus | clock pinned | clock free |
|---|---|---|---|
| `min-now` | hi `11,23` | 0.015 | 0.105 |
| `min-now` | lo `0,12` | 0.038 | 0.014 |
| `min-now` | none | 0.028 | 0.017 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | hi | 0.34 | 1.00 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | lo | 0.38 | 0.44 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | none | 5.03 | 4.43 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` | all six | 2.1 to 3.8 | 2.3 to 3.8 |

**Hypothesis 1, upper cpus give good results on the 3900X**
- Yes. With both pins on, `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` repeats to 0.34% and `min-now` to 0.015%.
- The lower pair `0,12` did as well: 0.38% and 0.038%. With eight invocations a spread is known only to about plus or minus 50%, so those are the same.
- What makes the difference is pinning the threads, not which pair they sit on. The host was idle for this hour, so a day with more housekeeping on cpu 0 could still separate them.
- The two "hi, free" outliers both come from round 1:
  - For `min-now`, round 1 read 24.150 ns and rounds 2 to 8 read 24.076 to 24.083.
  - For `zcr-spsc-v3-2t`, round 1 read 54.05 ns against about 52.6 after.
  - That was the second invocation of the whole session. This morning's run also had its disturbance in the first two minutes.
  - We think the first minute or two of any session should be a throwaway invocation.

**Hypothesis 2, unpinned is still poor**
- This is confirmed for the two-thread bench.
  - Unpinned `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` reads 119 to 133 ns where pinned reads 51 to 62.
  - Run means within one invocation span 114 to 367 ns.
  - The trimmed means wander by 12 to 15% across invocations.
  - It is a different measurement, since the scheduler puts the two threads on different cores each run.
- It is not confirmed for `min-now`, which has one thread and repeats to 0.017 to 0.028% unpinned, as good as pinned.
- The lag-1 autocorrelation of block means is near zero in every cell, -0.12 to +0.11. With ten blocks per run this data cannot test the earlier +0.78.

**Hypothesis 3, `--pin-freq` always gives smoother results**
- It is not smoother. It helped "hi" on both benches, was level on "lo" and "none" for the two-thread bench, and was slightly worse on "lo" and "none" for `min-now`, where every number is tiny anyway.
- What it buys is the trustworthy half of "trustworthy". For `zcr-spsc-v3-2t`, I counted how many of the 28 invocation pairs differ by more than their claimed `LSC trimmed`. About 1 or 2 of 28 should if the claim is honest:

| cpus | pinned | free |
|---|---|---|
| hi | 0 of 28 | 9 of 28 |
| lo | 3 of 28 | 6 of 28 |

- It also makes the number independent of the core.
  - With the clock free, core 11 boosts to 4.38 GHz and core 0 to 4.52.
  - So "hi" reads 52.8 ns and "lo" reads 50.7, a 4% difference that is only the clock.
  - Pinned, they read 61.594 and 61.602, identical to 0.01%.
- The cost is that a pinned number is 8 to 17% slower than the machine runs unpinned, because it is measured at 3.77 GHz.

**Two findings for the `analyze` rung**
- `min-now`'s claim fails in every condition.
  - The real spread is 1.4 to 12 times what `LSC trimmed` implies, and 4 to 11 of 28 pairs exceed it.
  - The four kept runs of one invocation agree to 0.004 ns, while invocations differ by 0.004 to 0.025 ns.
  - That is a between-invocation component no single invocation can see, which is exactly the case "checks a claim across invocations" is for.
  - In absolute terms it is a hundredth of a nanosecond.
- `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` sits on three levels in every condition.
  - Pinned, its runs land at about 17, 19 and 24.5 ns, split roughly 45/40/15.
  - Free, they land at 15.5, 17.5 and 22.5, which is the same three scaled by the clock ratio.
  - Neither pin changes the mix, so we think the level is set by where memory lands and not by the cpu or the clock.
  - Its `LSC trimmed` comes out at 6 to 11%, which is honest (0 or 1 of 28 exceed) and useless.
  - This morning's 0.009 ns claim was the lucky case where all four kept runs fell on one level.

**What this means for `iiac-perf.toml`**
- Pin the cpus by a profile name and pin the clock.
- At the short settings the 3900X then gives `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` a claimed `LSC trimmed` of about 1.1%, and that claim holds.
- That is twice the cycle's 0.5% target, so the short settings are honest on this host but not yet tight enough. We think that means more runs rather than longer ones, which the run-length rung can check.

**Limits**
- This is one session on one host, with eight invocations per cell and the SMT pair only.
- `ccx` was not tried, and the settings are untuned.

The plain version: locking the threads to a core pair is what makes this machine's numbers repeatable, and which pair mattered little today. Locking the clock doesn't make numbers smoother, but it makes their error bars believable and makes two different cores give the same answer. One of the three benches jumps between three speeds no matter what we pin, so its error bar is wide but truthful.

Three things for you to decide:
- **Tracking:** `records/pins.jsonl` is 7.2 MB. I lean towards tracking it, since it is the first data where a claim visibly fails and `analyze`'s tests will want it. `records/` would then total about 12 MB.
- **Warm-up invocation:** should `configs/pins.sh` and the claim loop each get a discarded first invocation?
- **`feat: a pins experiment on the 3900X` rung:** the scripts are `tmp/pins.py` and `tmp/pins2.py`, throwaway Python of the kind the `analyze` rung exists to replace. The findings above should go into `TODO.md`'s deliberation. That is a change to the cycle's plan, and the working copy already holds the config changes. I'd put it all in an inserted rung, something like `feat: a pins experiment on the 3900X`, before `analyze`. Do you want that?

message.content:
- Tracking: yes
- Warm-up invocation: no, with "trimed" at 10-50 "bad" entries will be trimed, hence we should not discard first.
- feat: a pins exper .. 3900x rung: yes

insert the rung.

min-now is not a real bench, it's to see if iiac-perf can measure a low cost bench, so IMO no decision should be made on it's behavior. It could be useful for comparing costs of individual instructions but by it self it simply shows we can measure a trivial bench.

I suggest we drop min-now from pins.sh and run it on 7600x and test all profiles a CPU.

One other thing I want the a set of runs to use as little wall time as possible to get comparable results and I want to use the resulting config to optimize zcr-mpsc-v2 and zc-spsc-v3 as best as possible.

Finally, I'm not answering the question "how fast is bench xyz", instead I want to create a "baseline config so changes to a bench can be reliably detected".

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# The pins experiment: what the cpu pin and the clock pin each buy, on this host.
#
# Every NAME=CPUS on the line is a cpu pin, and `none`, the unpinned case, is always one more.
# Each is crossed with the clock pin (pin, free), and each condition is an invocation of
# configs/pins.toml with its pins on the line and a tag for each factor, `cpus=NAME` and
# `freq=pin|free`. The conditions go round-robin, the start rotating each round, so a drift over
# the run lands on every condition alike and none always follows the same neighbor. Run from the
# repo root, and leave the host alone until it ends.
#
#   configs/pins.sh NAME=CPUS...
#   configs/pins.sh hi=11,23 lo=0,12                          # the 3900X rows of records/pins.jsonl
#   configs/pins.sh smt=11,23 ccx=11,10 x-ccx=11,8            # 3900X, every profile on the last core
#   configs/pins.sh smt=5,11 ccx=5,4 lo-smt=0,6 lo-ccx=0,1    # 7600X
#
# ROUNDS is the invocations of each condition, 8 by default. FREQ is the clock conditions,
# "pin free" by default, so FREQ=pin halves the run once the clock pin is settled. BIN names the
# binary, iiac-perf-dev while a cycle runs. An invocation of the four benches is about 85 s, so
# the 7600X line above is 10 conditions by 8 rounds, about 1 h 55 m.
set -euo pipefail

rounds=${ROUNDS:-8}
bin=${BIN:-iiac-perf-dev}
read -r -a freqs <<<"${FREQ:-pin free}"

if (($# == 0)); then
    echo "usage: configs/pins.sh NAME=CPUS..." >&2
    exit 2
fi

conditions=()
for pin in "$@" none=; do
    if [[ $pin != *=* ]]; then
        echo "error: '$pin' is not NAME=CPUS" >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    for freq in "${freqs[@]}"; do
        conditions+=("$pin $freq")
    done
done
n=${#conditions[@]}

for ((r = 0; r < rounds; r++)); do
    for ((i = 0; i < n; i++)); do
        read -r pin freq <<<"${conditions[(r + i) % n]}"
        name=${pin%%=*}
        cpus=${pin#*=}
        args=(configs/pins.toml --tag "cpus=$name" --tag "freq=$freq")
        if [[ -n $cpus ]]; then
            args+=(--pin-cpus "$cpus")
        fi
        if [[ $freq == pin ]]; then
            args+=(--pin-freq)
        fi
        echo "== round $((r + 1))/$rounds: cpus=$name${cpus:+ ($cpus)} freq=$freq"
        "$bin" "${args[@]}"
    done
done

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# The pins experiment: what the cpu pin and the clock pin each buy, on this host.
#
# Six conditions, the cpu pin (hi, lo, none) crossed with the clock pin (pin, free), each an
# invocation of configs/pins.toml with its pins on the line and a tag for each factor. The
# conditions go round-robin, the start rotating each round, so a drift over the hour lands on
# every condition alike and none always follows the same neighbor. Run from the repo root, and
# leave the host alone until it ends: 8 rounds of 6 is 48 invocations, about 50 minutes.
#
#   configs/pins.sh HI LO [ROUNDS]
#   configs/pins.sh 11,23 0,12      # 3900X: the last core's SMT pair against the first's
#   configs/pins.sh 5,11 0,6        # 7600X
#
# BIN names the binary, iiac-perf-dev while a cycle runs.
set -euo pipefail

hi=${1:?HI cpus, as 11,23}
lo=${2:?LO cpus, as 0,12}
rounds=${3:-8}
bin=${BIN:-iiac-perf-dev}

conditions=("hi pin" "hi free" "lo pin" "lo free" "none pin" "none free")
n=${#conditions[@]}

for ((r = 0; r < rounds; r++)); do
    for ((i = 0; i < n; i++)); do
        read -r cpus freq <<<"${conditions[(r + i) % n]}"
        args=(configs/pins.toml --tag "cpus=$cpus" --tag "freq=$freq")
        case $cpus in
        hi) args+=(--pin-cpus "$hi") ;;
        lo) args+=(--pin-cpus "$lo") ;;
        esac
        if [[ $freq == pin ]]; then
            args+=(--pin-freq)
        fi
        echo "== round $((r + 1))/$rounds: cpus=$cpus freq=$freq"
        "$bin" "${args[@]}"
    done
done

anchor='\n#### Ladder details\n'

s=s.replace(anchor,delib.rstrip('\n')+'\n'+anchor,1)
detail='''##### feat: a pins experiment on the 3900X

An inserted rung (wink, 2026-09-19), from three hypotheses: that the 3900X gives good results on
its upper cpus, that it still gives poor ones unpinned, and that `--pin-freq` always gives
smoother ones. `configs/pins.toml` is the short settings with no pin of either kind, and
`configs/pins.sh` crosses every cpu pin named on its line, and the unpinned case, with the clock
pinned and free, round-robin with a rotating start so a drift lands on every condition alike.
The 3900X session is `records/pins.jsonl`: `hi=11,23`, `lo=0,12`, and `none`, 8 invocations of 10
runs of each, 48 invocations in 58 minutes with nobody at the host.

- The cpu pin is what makes a two-thread bench repeatable, and which pair mattered little: the
  spread of the 8 trimmed means of `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` is 0.34% on `hi` and 0.38% on `lo`, clock
  pinned, where 8 invocations fix a spread to about half its value. We think a busier day could
  still separate them, the host having idled through the hour.
- Unpinned is poor for two threads and fine for one. `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` reads 119 to 133 ns against
  51 to 62 pinned, one invocation's runs spanning 114 to 367 ns and the trimmed means 12 to 15%,
  so it is another measurement, the scheduler placing the pair afresh each run.
- The clock pin buys calibration, not smoothness. Of the 28 pairs of invocations of
  `zcr-spsc-v3-2t`, those further apart than their `LSC trimmed` are 0 on `hi` and 3 on `lo`
  pinned, against 9 and 6 free, where an honest claim allows 1 or 2. The spreads themselves are
  0.34% against 1.00% on `hi` and 0.38% against 0.44% on `lo`, so "always smoother" fails.
- The clock pin also makes the number the same on any core: free, core 11 boosts to 4.38 GHz and
  core 0 to 4.52, so `hi` reads 52.8 ns and `lo` 50.7, and pinned they read 61.594 and 61.602.
- At the short settings the pinned pair claims an `LSC trimmed` of about 1.1% for
  `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` and keeps it, twice the 0.5% target, so the settings are honest here and not
  yet tight.
- `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` sits on three levels in every condition, near 17, 19, and 24.5 ns pinned, about
  45, 40, and 15 runs of 100, and the same three scaled by the clock when free. Neither pin moves
  the mix, so we think the level is where the memory lands. Its `LSC trimmed` is 6 to 11%, true
  and of no use, and the 0.009 ns it claimed the day before was four kept runs on one level.
  [Mark a run that lands on another level](#mark-a-run-that-lands-on-another-level) is where a
  baseline for this bench has to come from.
- The block lag-1 is near zero in every cell, -0.12 to +0.11, and ten blocks cannot test the
  +0.78 the unpinned 3900X showed at a hundred.
- The numbers came from throwaway Python, which
  [feat: analyze checks a claim across invocations][7] replaces, and this file is the first
  where a claim visibly fails, so that rung's tests take it.
- The script now takes `NAME=CPUS` pairs, so one line tests every profile of a host, and the
  benches are the two rings with `min-now` dropped. The 7600X session is run from there once
  this rung is pushed, and is a rung of its own.
- Also here, since they are what the experiment ran on: `configs/claim.toml`, the same three
  benches under `pin_cpus = "smt"` for the 20-invocation check of one claim, not yet run, two
  7600X configs moved into `configs/` with a copied 3900X `[freq]` taken out, and the screen
  capture of the unrecorded run that started this, under `records/screens/`.
- Two entries went to `## Todo`, a `setup-host` command and `init-config` printing TOML when
  asked.

'''
anchor2='##### feat: analyze checks a claim across invocations\n'
assert s.count(anchor2)==1
s=s.replace(anchor2,detail+anchor2,1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
awk 'length>100{print FILENAME": "FNR": "length}' TODO.md | head

Yes, your rationale for dropping `min-now` is sound, with one caveat.

**`min-now`**
- The goal is to detect changes to the rings. `min-now` is one thread reading a clock, with no ring, no second thread and no memory traffic, so it can't show how a ring's measurement behaves.
- The data agrees. `min-now` repeated to 0.017 to 0.028% even unpinned, the condition where the two-thread bench fell apart. Every one of its conditions looked "good" or "bad" at the hundredth-of-a-nanosecond scale.
  - My "its claim fails in every condition" finding was true, but it bears on nothing you want to decide.
- The caveat is that `min-now` is a good instrument check.
  - A `min-now` that stops reading about 26.16 ns pinned on this host means the harness or the host changed, not a bench.
  - So I would keep it out of experiments and decisions but not delete the bench.
  - I also would not call it the "confirmation", as the acceptance check still does.
- I recorded that in the deliberation under your name and left the acceptance check text for the closing to take up.

**The inserted rung `feat: a pins experiment on the 3900X`**
- It is marked `(current)` and sits before `analyze`. The ladder's link references are renumbered.
- The version-of-record is bumped to `0.28.17-5`.
- `records/pins.jsonl` is tracked.
  - It is 6.8 MiB, over jj's 5 MiB limit for new files, so I snapshotted it once with `--config snapshot.max-new-file-size=7200000` for that command only.
  - No repo setting changed.
- `configs/pins.sh` now takes `NAME=CPUS` pairs and always adds `none`.
  - The 3900X data reproduces as `configs/pins.sh hi=11,23 lo=0,12`.
  - The 7600X run is `configs/pins.sh smt=5,11 ccx=5,4 lo-smt=0,6 lo-ccx=0,1`.
  - `ROUNDS` and `FREQ` are environment settings. `FREQ=pin` halves a run once the clock pin is settled.
  - I dry-ran it with `echo` as the binary. The rotation and the argument errors behave.
- `configs/pins.toml` now names `zcr-mpsc-v2` and `zcr-spsc-v3`, four benches, without `min-now`. Its header says the 3900X rows were recorded under the earlier three benches.
- `.gitignore` lost the `/iiac-perf.md` rule, which contradicted a tracked `iiac-perf.toml`.
  - That reverses the rule's own comment, "each checkout's own project-local config".
  - I recorded it in the deliberation as a decision with its cost: a checkout that still holds an ignored `iiac-perf.md` fails after the pull until that file is removed.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Print every number in notes/pins-experiment.md from a pins record file.

    python3 configs/pins.py records/pins.jsonl

Temporary, as configs/knobs.py is: `analyze` takes its place, and until then this re-implements
the 10-50 trim and the `LSC trimmed` of src/series.rs for ten runs, so it refuses any other count.
"""

import json
import math
import statistics as st
import sys
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

RUNS = 10
T975_DF6 = 2.447  # t(0.975, 2 * kept - 2), kept = 4


def trimmed(means):
    """The mean of the 10th to 50th percentile of ten sorted means, the second to the fifth."""
    s = sorted(means)
    return sum(s[1:5]) / 4


def lsc_trimmed(means):
    """src/series.rs: t * se * sqrt(2), se the winsorized stdev over (kept / n) * sqrt(n)."""
    s = sorted(means)
    w = [min(max(m, s[1]), s[4]) for m in means]
    se = st.stdev(w) / (0.4 * math.sqrt(RUNS))
    return T975_DF6 * se * math.sqrt(2)


def lag1(x):
    m = sum(x) / len(x)
    d = sum((a - m) ** 2 for a in x)
    return sum((x[i] - m) * (x[i + 1] - m) for i in range(len(x) - 1)) / d if d > 0 else None


def main(path):
    runs = defaultdict(list)  # (bench, cpus, freq, series) -> run means
    ghz = defaultdict(list)
    lags = defaultdict(list)
    for line in open(path):
        try:
            r = json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            continue  # a crash mid-append leaves a broken last line
        cell = (r["bench"], r["tags"]["cpus"], r["tags"]["freq"])
        runs[cell + (r["series"],)].append(r["mean_ns"])
        ghz[cell].append(sum(r["clock_khz"]) / len(r["clock_khz"]) / 1e6)
        lag = lag1(r["block_mean_ns"])
        if lag is not None:
            lags[cell].append(lag)

    cells = defaultdict(list)  # cell -> [(trimmed mean, claimed LSC, run means)] in session order
    for key in sorted(runs, key=lambda k: k[3]):
        means = runs[key]
        if len(means) != RUNS:
            sys.exit(f"{key}: {len(means)} runs, and the trim here is written for {RUNS}")
        cells[key[:3]].append((trimmed(means), lsc_trimmed(means), means))

    print("Per cell: the grand trimmed mean, the spread and range of the invocations' trimmed")
    print("means, the mean claimed LSC trimmed, the pairs of invocations further apart than their")
    print("claim (about 5% if it holds), a run's spread, the clock, and the block lag-1.\n")
    print(
        f"{'bench':16}{'cpus':8}{'freq':6}{'inv':>4}{'trimmed':>10}{'sd%':>8}{'range%':>8}"
        f"{'LSC%':>8}{'exceed':>8}{'run sd%':>9}{'GHz':>7}{'lag1':>7}"
    )
    last = None
    for cell in sorted(cells):
        v = cells[cell]
        t = [x[0] for x in v]
        g = st.mean(t)
        pairs = [(a, b) for i, a in enumerate(v) for b in v[i + 1 :]]
        exceed = sum(abs(a[0] - b[0]) > math.sqrt((a[1] ** 2 + b[1] ** 2) / 2) for a, b in pairs)
        run_sd = st.mean(st.stdev(x[2]) for x in v)
        if last not in (None, cell[0]):
            print()
        last = cell[0]
        print(
            f"{cell[0]:16}{cell[1]:8}{cell[2]:6}{len(v):4}{g:10.3f}{st.stdev(t) / g * 100:8.3f}"
            f"{(max(t) - min(t)) / g * 100:8.2f}{st.mean(x[1] for x in v) / g * 100:8.3f}"
            f"{exceed:5}/{len(pairs):<2}{run_sd / g * 100:9.2f}{st.mean(ghz[cell]):7.3f}"
            f"{st.mean(lags[cell]):7.2f}"
        )

    print("\nEach cell's trimmed means in session order:\n")
    for cell in sorted(cells):
        print(f"{cell[0]:16}{cell[1]:8}{cell[2]:6}" + " ".join(f"{x[0]:.3f}" for x in cells[cell]))

    print("\nEach cell's run means, counted to the nearest 0.5 ns, where the levels show:\n")
    for cell in sorted(cells):
        counts = Counter(round(m * 2) / 2 for x in cells[cell] for m in x[2])
        if len(counts) <= 12:
            row = " ".join(f"{ns:g}:{n}" for ns, n in sorted(counts.items()))
            print(f"{cell[0]:16}{cell[1]:8}{cell[2]:6}{row}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    main(sys.argv[1])

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Print every number in notes/pins-experiment.md from a pins record file.

    python3 configs/pins.py records/pins.jsonl

Temporary, as configs/knobs.py is: `analyze` takes its place, and until then this re-implements
the 10-50 trim and the `LSC trimmed` of src/series.rs for ten runs, so it refuses any other count.
"""

import json
import math
import statistics as st
import sys
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

RUNS = 10
T975_DF6 = 2.447  # t(0.975, 2 * kept - 2), kept = 4


def trimmed(means):
    """The mean of the 10th to 50th percentile of ten sorted means, the second to the fifth."""
    s = sorted(means)
    return sum(s[1:5]) / 4


def lsc_trimmed(means):
    """src/series.rs: t * se * sqrt(2), se the winsorized stdev over (kept / n) * sqrt(n)."""
    s = sorted(means)
    w = [min(max(m, s[1]), s[4]) for m in means]
    se = st.stdev(w) / (0.4 * math.sqrt(RUNS))
    return T975_DF6 * se * math.sqrt(2)


def lag1(x):
    m = sum(x) / len(x)
    d = sum((a - m) ** 2 for a in x)
    return sum((x[i] - m) * (x[i + 1] - m) for i in range(len(x) - 1)) / d if d > 0 else None


def main(path):
    runs = defaultdict(list)  # (bench, cpus, freq, series) -> run means
    ghz = defaultdict(list)
    lags = defaultdict(list)
    for line in open(path):
        try:
            r = json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            continue  # a crash mid-append leaves a broken last line
        cell = (r["bench"], r["tags"]["cpus"], r["tags"]["freq"])
        runs[cell + (r["series"],)].append(r["mean_ns"])
        ghz[cell].append(sum(r["clock_khz"]) / len(r["clock_khz"]) / 1e6)
        lag = lag1(r["block_mean_ns"])
        if lag is not None:
            lags[cell].append(lag)

    cells = defaultdict(list)  # cell -> [(trimmed mean, claimed LSC, run means)] in session order
    for key in sorted(runs, key=lambda k: k[3]):
        means = runs[key]
        if len(means) != RUNS:
            sys.exit(f"{key}: {len(means)} runs, and the trim here is written for {RUNS}")
        cells[key[:3]].append((trimmed(means), lsc_trimmed(means), means))

    print("Per cell: the grand trimmed mean, the spread and range of the invocations' trimmed")
    print("means, the mean claimed LSC trimmed, the pairs of invocations further apart than their")
    print("claim (about 5% if it holds), a run's spread, the clock, and the block lag-1.\n")
    print(
        f"{'bench':16}{'cpus':8}{'freq':6}{'inv':>4}{'trimmed':>10}{'sd%':>8}{'range%':>8}"
        f"{'LSC%':>8}{'exceed':>8}{'run sd%':>9}{'GHz':>7}{'lag1':>7}"
    )
    last = None
    for cell in sorted(cells):
        v = cells[cell]
        t = [x[0] for x in v]
        g = st.mean(t)
        pairs = [(a, b) for i, a in enumerate(v) for b in v[i + 1 :]]
        exceed = sum(abs(a[0] - b[0]) > math.sqrt((a[1] ** 2 + b[1] ** 2) / 2) for a, b in pairs)
        run_sd = st.mean(st.stdev(x[2]) for x in v)
        if last not in (None, cell[0]):
            print()
        last = cell[0]
        print(
            f"{cell[0]:16}{cell[1]:8}{cell[2]:6}{len(v):4}{g:10.3f}{st.stdev(t) / g * 100:8.3f}"
            f"{(max(t) - min(t)) / g * 100:8.2f}{st.mean(x[1] for x in v) / g * 100:8.3f}"
            f"{exceed:5}/{len(pairs):<2}{run_sd / g * 100:9.2f}{st.mean(ghz[cell]):7.3f}"
            f"{st.mean(lags[cell]):7.2f}"
        )

    print("\nEach cell's trimmed means in session order:\n")
    for cell in sorted(cells):
        print(f"{cell[0]:16}{cell[1]:8}{cell[2]:6}" + " ".join(f"{x[0]:.3f}" for x in cells[cell]))

    print("\nEach cell's run means, counted to the nearest 0.5 ns, where the levels show:\n")
    for cell in sorted(cells):
        counts = Counter(round(m * 2) / 2 for x in cells[cell] for m in x[2])
        if len(counts) <= 12:
            row = " ".join(f"{ns:g}:{n}" for ns, n in sorted(counts.items()))
            print(f"{cell[0]:16}{cell[1]:8}{cell[2]:6}{row}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:

# The pins experiment

What the cpu pin and the clock pin each buy a run, measured by whether a config's claim about
itself, `LSC trimmed`, holds when the same config is invoked again. It serves the baseline
config, the one under which a change between a bench and a modification of it is detected
reliably in the least wall time, so what counts is a claim that is small and true, never how
fast a bench is. Each host's session is a section here, added by the rung that ran it.

## Recreating it

Everything a session needs is tracked, and every record carries its own config, host, version,
and tags, so a line of `records/pins.jsonl` says what produced it.

- Settings: [configs/pins.toml](../configs/pins.toml), the short settings and no pin of either
  kind.
- Conditions: [configs/pins.sh](../configs/pins.sh) crosses each `NAME=CPUS` on its line, and
  `none`, with the clock pinned and free, tags each invocation `cpus=NAME` and `freq=pin|free`,
  and goes round-robin with a rotating start so a drift lands on every condition alike. The host
  is left alone until it ends.
- Records: `records/pins.jsonl`, every session appended, told apart by `host.name` and the tags.
- Numbers: `python3 configs/pins.py records/pins.jsonl` prints every number below. It is
  temporary, as `configs/knobs.py` is, and `analyze` takes its place.
- A host needs a `[freq]` table in its XDG config for the clock pin, which `setup-freq` writes.

## 3900X, 2026-09-19

`configs/pins.sh hi=11,23 lo=0,12`, 8 rounds, 48 invocations of 10 runs in 48 minutes, under
0.28.17-4 and the bench list of that day, `zcr-spsc-v3-2t`, `min-now`, and `zcr-spsc-v3-1t`.
`hi` is the last core's SMT pair and `lo` the first's. The hypotheses were wink's: the upper
cpus give good results even here, unpinned still gives poor ones, and `--pin-freq` always gives
smoother ones.

`sd` and `range` are of a cell's 8 trimmed means, `LSC` the mean claim, and `exceed` the pairs of
invocations further apart than their claim, 1 or 2 of 28 when it holds.

| bench | cpus | freq | trimmed ns | sd % | range % | LSC % | exceed |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | hi | pin | 61.594 | 0.338 | 0.82 | 1.096 | 0/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | hi | free | 52.802 | 0.999 | 3.21 | 0.985 | 9/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | lo | pin | 61.602 | 0.378 | 1.00 | 1.156 | 3/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | lo | free | 50.727 | 0.441 | 1.32 | 0.991 | 6/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | none | pin | 132.739 | 5.027 | 14.76 | 18.005 | 3/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | none | free | 119.360 | 4.434 | 12.17 | 16.804 | 0/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` | hi | pin | 17.394 | 2.143 | 6.20 | 11.069 | 0/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` | hi | free | 16.083 | 3.542 | 9.50 | 8.177 | 0/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` | lo | pin | 17.580 | 3.424 | 9.89 | 10.392 | 0/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` | lo | free | 15.952 | 2.314 | 6.18 | 6.795 | 1/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` | none | pin | 17.380 | 2.838 | 6.31 | 6.451 | 0/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` | none | free | 16.133 | 3.818 | 9.26 | 6.140 | 0/28 |

- The cpu pin is what makes a two-thread bench repeatable, and which pair mattered little:
  0.34% on `hi` and 0.38% on `lo`, clock pinned, where 8 invocations fix a spread to about half
  its value. We think a busier day could still separate them, the host having idled throughout.
- Unpinned is poor for two threads, another measurement and not a noisier one: the scheduler
  places the pair afresh each run, so one invocation's runs span 114 to 367 ns.
- The clock pin buys calibration, not smoothness. Pinned, 0 and 3 pairs of 28 break the claim,
  and free, 9 and 6. The spreads are better on `hi` and level on `lo`, so "always smoother"
  fails.
- The clock pin makes the number the same on any core. Free, core 11 boosts to 4.38 GHz and core
  0 to 4.52 under this bench, so `hi` reads 52.8 ns and `lo` 50.7, and pinned they agree to
  0.01%. The price is a number 8 to 17% above the boosted one, which a comparison never sees.
- The short settings claim about 1.1% for `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` pinned and keep it, twice the 0.5% a
  baseline wants, so they are honest here and not yet tight.
- `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` sits on three levels in every condition, near 17, 19, and 24.5 ns pinned,
  about 45, 45, and 10 runs of 100, and the same three scaled by the clock when free. Neither
  pin moves the mix, so we think the level is where the memory lands. Its claim of 6 to 11% is
  true and of no use, and a baseline for it waits on telling the levels apart.
- `min-now` was repeatable to 0.03% in every condition, the unpinned one included, so it cannot
  tell the conditions apart, and later sessions leave it out.
- The block lag-1 is near zero everywhere, -0.12 to +0.11, and ten blocks cannot test the +0.78
  the unpinned host showed at a hundred.

What it does not say: one session, one idle hour, the SMT pair alone with `ccx` and `x-ccx`
untried, and settings nobody has tuned, so a poor cell is poor at 0.25 s and ten blocks.

content.text:
I corrected both points in the deliberation, and the experiment now has a durable write-up and tracked tools to recreate it.

**Your two corrections**
- The goal bullet now reads "a change between any baseline bench and a modification of it is detected reliably, in the least wall time". Optimizing `zcr-mpsc-v2` and `zcr-spsc-v3` is recorded as its first use and explicitly not the config's scope.
- The `min-now` bullet now says only that it is not in the pins experiment. It gives the reason from the data: `min-now` was repeatable to 0.03% in every condition, unpinned included, so it cannot tell the conditions apart.
  - The bullet says `min-now` stays a bench and that what the acceptance check asks of it is unchanged.
  - I removed my overreach about superseding `min-now` in the acceptance check.

**Where the results are recorded**
- The `TODO.md` block is the wrong home for them. It is deleted at the next cycle's opening, and the protocol says findings that must outlive a cycle go into `notes/` by the rung that made them.
- So I wrote `notes/pins-experiment.md` and indexed it from `notes/README.md`. It holds:
  - the question;
  - a "Recreating it" section;
  - one section per host session.
- The 3900X section has the exact command line, the date, the binary version, the bench list of that day, the full table, the findings, and what the session does not show.
- The 7600X session becomes a second section, added by its own rung.

**What recreates the experiment, all tracked**
- Settings: `configs/pins.toml`.
- Conditions: `configs/pins.sh`, where the 3900X data is `configs/pins.sh hi=11,23 lo=0,12`.
- Data: `records/pins.jsonl`.
  - Every session is appended to the one file.
  - Each line carries its own config, host, version and tags, so a record says what produced it without the note.
- Numbers: `python3 configs/pins.py records/pins.jsonl` prints every number in the note.
  - I consolidated my two throwaway scripts into this one.
  - It reads the conditions from the tags instead of hard-coding them.
  - It refuses any run count other than ten, since it re-implements the trim for ten.
  - I ran it and it reproduces the figures I reported.
- This follows the repo's precedent. `docs/report-guide.md` says of the clock-shift data "`python3 configs/clock-shift.py records/clock-shift.jsonl` prints every number here".
- You don't want Python in the repo. `configs/pins.py` is marked temporary in its header and in the note, exactly as `configs/knobs.py` is. The `analyze` rung is where all three scripts go, and its tests take this file.
- If you would rather not track it even for one rung, say so and I'll drop it. The cost is that the note's numbers can't be regenerated until `analyze` lands.

**Two small fixes along the way**
- The level split for `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` is about 45, 45 and 10 runs of 100, not the 45, 40 and 15 I first wrote. I recounted it from the script output.
- The example lines in `configs/pins.sh` are back inside 100 columns.

content.text:
I'd go with one separate repo for all experiments rather than a repo per experiment. There is one decision to make before this rung is pushed, because pushing `records/pins.jsonl` here can't be undone.

**Why moving experiments out of this repo makes sense**
- **Size:**
  - `records/` is already 4.7 MB in this repo's history, and `pins.jsonl` adds 7 MB.
  - The 7600X session would add about 14 MB more: four benches, ten conditions, eight rounds.
  - Git never forgets a pushed file, so the tool's repo would carry every experiment forever.
- **Python:** you don't want it here, and an experiment's analysis script is exactly the kind of Python that keeps arriving.
- **Lifecycle:**
  - An experiment is a question asked of one version of the tool.
  - Its records already carry that version, so it doesn't need to live beside the source.
- **The protocol:**
  - This rung is an experiment wedged into a feature cycle titled for another host.
  - It pulled config moves, a `.gitignore` reversal and a notes file along with it.
  - An experiment wants its own small cycle, not a ladder rung in the tool's.

**Why not one repo per experiment**
- Each repo in this family is a work-repo plus an agent-repo, with its own agent-files, bookmarks, and push approvals.
- A dozen small experiments would mean a dozen of those.
- Experiments get compared with each other.
  - The pins and claim experiments share benches and settings on purpose.
  - Across repos that comparison needs two checkouts and sha-links.
- A pattern learned in one experiment, such as the round-robin script or the write-up shape, would have to be copied rather than reused.

**What I'd do instead**
- One repo, say `iiac-perf-experiments`, with a directory per experiment.
- `pins/` would hold `README.md` (the note I just wrote), `pins.toml`, `pins.sh`, the analysis script, and `records/`.
- The directory is the unit and is self-contained, so splitting one out later costs little.
- This repo keeps the tool, the shipped configs (`iiac-perf.toml` and the example), and small record fixtures for `analyze`'s tests.
  - A fixture is a slice of an experiment, not the experiment itself.
  - The two `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` cells that show a claim holding and failing are 160 records, about 0.7 MB.

**The decision that can't wait**
- If experiments are leaving this repo, `records/pins.jsonl` should not go into this push. Once pushed, it stays in history whatever we decide later.
- Everything else in the working copy is small and can move afterwards at no cost.

**How I'd sequence it, if you agree**
1. This rung shrinks to the config and host-fact changes.
   - It drops the experiment's data, script, Python, and note from the commit.
   - Those stay on disk, untracked, until the new repo exists.
   - The rung's title would change to match, since it is not yet pushed.
2. The experiments repo gets created (`vc-x1 init`, its agent-files). That is its own piece of work and yours to start.
3. `pins/` becomes its first experiment. The 7600X session is run from there.
4. The `analyze` rung takes a small fixture slice, not the whole file.

That is a change to the agreed plan, so I've touched nothing.

Two questions:
- One experiments repo, or do you still prefer one per experiment?
- Should I keep `records/pins.jsonl` out of this rung's commit?

The plain version: experiment data is big and permanent once pushed, and it doesn't belong in the tool's history. A single sibling repo with a folder per experiment gets you that separation without the overhead of a new repo every time. What needs deciding now is whether the 7 MB file goes into this push.

content.text:
Dropping the one-thread benches from the pins experiment is right, with one caveat below. `records/pins.jsonl` is out of this rung's commit, and everything belonging to the experiment is staged on disk for the new experiments repo.

**Dropping the `-1t` benches**
- I agree. A pin experiment asks where a pair of threads should sit. One thread has no pair, so the cpu factor tells it nothing, and the data showed that.
- Wall time falls too. An invocation drops from about 85 s to about 45 s, and the 7600X session of ten conditions by eight rounds drops from nearly two hours to about one.
- The caveat: `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` showed three levels that neither pin moves, which makes its claim useless at 6 to 11%.
  - That is the largest obstacle the data found to detecting a change in any bench.
  - Dropping `-1t` from this experiment is right, but the question should not be dropped with it.
  - It has a home already, the Todo `### Mark a run that lands on another level`.

cd /home/wink/data/prgs/rust/iiac-perf && python3 - <<'EOF'
p='tmp/experiments/pins/README.md'; s=open(p).read()
tail='What it does not say: one session'
a=s.index(tail)
old_tail=s[a:]
sec='''## 3900X, 2026-09-19, every profile

`./pins.sh smt=11,23 ccx=11,10 x-ccx=11,8 lo-smt=0,12 lo-ccx=0,1`, 8 rounds, 96 invocations of 10
runs in 65 minutes, under 0.28.17-4, on `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` and `zcr-spsc-v3-2t`.
`python3 pins.py records/pins.jsonl 3900x 2026-09-19T18` prints it. The pairs are the placements
rule's on the last core, and the first core's `smt` and `ccx` beside them.

Clock pinned:

| bench | cpus | trimmed ns | sd % | range % | LSC % | exceed |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` | smt | 65.337 | 0.254 | 0.61 | 0.721 | 0/28 |
| `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` | lo-smt | 65.344 | 0.217 | 0.61 | 0.682 | 1/28 |
| `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` | ccx | 122.370 | 0.247 | 0.80 | 0.354 | 7/28 |
| `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` | lo-ccx | 124.079 | 0.147 | 0.50 | 0.304 | 1/28 |
| `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` | x-ccx | 397.297 | 0.060 | 0.19 | 0.298 | 0/28 |
| `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` | none | 127.790 | 6.538 | 19.55 | 4.318 | 9/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | smt | 61.473 | 0.159 | 0.49 | 0.821 | 0/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | lo-smt | 61.486 | 0.330 | 0.81 | 0.757 | 0/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | ccx | 122.880 | 0.279 | 0.87 | 0.888 | 0/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | lo-ccx | 122.161 | 0.295 | 0.84 | 1.184 | 0/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | x-ccx | 367.009 | 0.191 | 0.64 | 0.512 | 3/28 |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | none | 127.868 | 3.004 | 9.55 | 12.331 | 0/28 |

Clock free, the same cells: `exceed` is 4, 3, 2, 2, 6, and 2 of 28 for `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` and 2, 5,
11, 5, 3, and 3 for `zcr-spsc-v3-2t`, and the spreads run 0.23 to 0.78% pinned to a core pair.

- The profile is what is measured, not how well: `smt` reads 61 and 65 ns, `ccx` 122 and 123,
  and `x-ccx` 367 and 397. The template calls `ccx` "the best channel latency", and for these
  rings the SMT pair, sharing an L1 and L2, is twice as fast. A baseline names one profile and
  a comparison never crosses them.
- Every pinned profile repeats to 0.06 to 0.33% between invocations, the last core and the first
  alike, so on this host any pinned pair serves a baseline and the choice is what to measure.
- The session agrees with the morning's across six hours: `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` on `11,23` pinned
  read 61.594 then and 61.473 now, 0.2% apart under claims of 0.8 to 1.1%.
- The clock pin buys calibration again, 11 of the 12 pinned cells at 3 of 28 or under against 7
  of the 12 free. The exception is `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` on `ccx`, 7 of 28: its trimmed means climb
  from 121.9 to 122.9 ns over the hour, as `lo-ccx` and `x-ccx` do by less, a slow drift between
  invocations that no invocation's own runs can see. We think it is temperature. It is the case
  `analyze` exists for, and an A/B that alternates its two sides is what cancels it.
- Unpinned is again another measurement, 115 to 128 ns with runs spread over 50%.
- The claims pinned are 0.3 to 1.2%, so the short settings reach the 0.5% target on some cells
  and miss it on `smt`, the fastest, by less than twofold.

'''
s=s[:a]+old_tail.rstrip('\n')+'\n\n'+sec
# move the first session's limits line to stay with its section: it already precedes the new section
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
awk 'length>100{print FILENAME": "FNR}' tmp/experiments/pins/README.md; rg -n "^## " tmp/experiments/pins/README.md
