content.text:
The second 3900X session is finished and written up. The 7600X session is still running, so nothing about that host is in yet.

**7600X: a false start that cost an hour**
- The first launch died at its first invocation with `record: opening …/records/pins.jsonl: No such file or directory`.
  - `iiac-perf` opens the record file but does not create its directory.
  - My smoke test had used a directory-style record, which does get created, so it didn't catch this.
- `pins.sh` now runs `mkdir -p records`.
- I relaunched at 19:16Z, and 84 records had arrived cleanly a few minutes later.
- My relaunch kept an ssh connection open for about three minutes before I closed it. The first round or so of that session had that contact.
- It should end around 20:20Z.
- A local timer wakes me at 20:25Z; then I'll look once and copy the records over.

**3900X, every profile**
- The session was 96 invocations in 65 minutes with no errors, under 0.28.17-4.
- Conditions: the three last-core pairs (`smt` `11,23`, `ccx` `11,10`, `x-ccx` `11,8`), the two first-core pairs (`lo-smt` `0,12`, `lo-ccx` `0,1`), and `none`. The table is the clock-pinned cells.
- Benches: `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` and `zcr-spsc-v3-2t`.

| cpus | `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` ns | spread % | `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` ns | spread % |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| smt `11,23` | 65.3 | 0.25 | 61.5 | 0.16 |
| lo-smt `0,12` | 65.3 | 0.22 | 61.5 | 0.33 |
| ccx `11,10` | 122.4 | 0.25 | 122.9 | 0.28 |
| lo-ccx `0,1` | 124.1 | 0.15 | 122.2 | 0.30 |
| x-ccx `11,8` | 397.3 | 0.06 | 367.0 | 0.19 |
| none | 127.8 | 6.5 | 127.9 | 3.0 |

- **The profile decides what is measured, not how well.**
  - `smt` reads about 61 to 65 ns, `ccx` about 122, and `x-ccx` 367 to 397.
  - The template calls `ccx` "the best channel latency". For these rings the SMT pair, which shares an L1 and L2 cache, is twice as fast.
  - So a baseline has to name one profile, and a comparison must never cross profiles.
- **Every pinned pair repeats to 0.06 to 0.33% between invocations.**
  - That holds on the first core as well as the last.
  - Your upper-cpus hypothesis holds, but on this host it is pinning that buys repeatability, not which pair.
- **The two sessions agree six hours apart.**
  - `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` on `11,23` pinned read 61.594 ns this morning and 61.473 ns now.
  - That is 0.2% apart, under claims of 0.8 to 1.1%.
- **The clock pin buys calibration again.**
  - Pinned, 10 of 12 cells have 3 or fewer of 28 invocation pairs further apart than their `LSC trimmed` claim, against 7 of 12 with the clock free.
  - One failure is the unpinned `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t`. The other is `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` on `ccx`.
- **`zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` on `ccx` drifts.**
  - Its trimmed means climb from 121.9 to 122.9 ns over the hour.
  - `lo-ccx` and `x-ccx` show the same pattern more weakly.
  - It is a slow drift between invocations that no single invocation can see, and we think it is temperature.
  - For your goal it means an A/B comparison should alternate its two sides so the drift cancels, as `pins.sh` alternates its conditions.
  - It is also exactly what `analyze` has to check across invocations.
- **Claims at the short settings are 0.3 to 1.2% pinned.** Some cells already meet the 0.5% target. `smt`, the fastest profile, misses it by less than twofold.

**Files changed, all under `tmp/experiments/pins/`**
- `README.md` has a new section for this session.
- `pins.py` takes an optional host and a time window, so one session of a multi-session file prints alone: `python3 pins.py records/pins.jsonl 3900x 2026-09-19T18`.
- `pins.sh` creates `records/`.

Nothing in the repo's tracked files changed. The rung `chore: host facts leave the project configs` is still at its work review, unpushed.

**Worth a Todo when you're back:** `iiac-perf` could create a record file's parent directory, as it already does for a record directory. I have not added one.

content.text:
The relaunched 7600X session ran to completion with no errors: all 80 invocations in 54 minutes, 1600 records. I checked it once after it ended.
- I fetched the records and appended them to `tmp/experiments/pins/records/pins.jsonl`, which now holds 3360 lines from the 3900X and 1600 from the 7600X.
- Both benches were pinned at 4701 MHz.

| cpus | `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` ns | spread % | claim % | `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` ns | spread % | claim % |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| smt `5,11` | 46.9 | 0.09 | 0.19 | 51.2 | 0.59 | 2.1 |
| lo-smt `0,6` | 46.9 | 0.07 | 0.15 | 51.5 | 0.53 | 3.1 |
| ccx `5,4` | 76.9 | 0.15 | 0.49 | 96.7 | 0.14 | 0.56 |
| lo-ccx `0,1` | 76.7 | 0.27 | 0.49 | 95.4 | 0.13 | 0.59 |
| none | 76.8 | 0.30 | 0.90 | 94.9 | 0.67 | 1.26 |

"Spread" is how far the eight invocations' trimmed means sit apart. "Claim" is the `LSC trimmed` that each invocation reports for itself.

**`zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` on the SMT pair already has its baseline.**
- Invocations sit 0.07 to 0.09% apart under a claim of 0.15 to 0.19%.
- All 80 runs fall between 46.5 and 48 ns.
- That beats the 0.5% target by about threefold at the short settings, with an invocation of about 45 s for the two benches.

**`zcr-spsc-v3-2t` on the same pair is the worst pinned cell.**
- The claim is honest: no invocation pair broke it. But at 2 to 3% it is wide.
- Its 80 runs on `5,11` smear from 50.6 to 53.1 ns. We think that is four sub-levels near 50.7, 51.1, 52.1 and 52.7.
- Eight more runs sit in a tail from 54 to 80 ns.
- The trim removes the tail, and the smear is what is left. We think more runs would tighten this claim, and longer runs would not.
- On `ccx` the same bench is tight: 0.14% spread under a 0.56% claim.
- So the `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` baseline works on `ccx` today. On `smt` it needs either more runs or an explanation of the sub-levels.

**Unpinned is not poor on the 7600X.**
- It reads the same as `ccx`: 76.8 against 76.9 ns for `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t`, and 94.9 against 96.7 ns for `zcr-spsc-v3-2t`.
- The 7600X has one L3, so the scheduler can only place the pair on two cores of it.
- It repeats to 0.3 to 0.7%, where the unpinned 3900X wandered 3 to 20%.
- So your second hypothesis is about the 3900X's four L3s, not a general rule.
- Pinning is still the better choice. The pinned `ccx` cells are tighter for `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` and no worse than unpinned for `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t`.

**The profile decides what is measured, on both hosts.**
- On the 7600X, `smt` reads 47 and 51 ns against 77 and 96 ns for `ccx`.
- On the 3900X, `smt` reads 65 and 61 ns against 122 and 123 ns for `ccx`.
- The last core against the first makes no difference on either host.

**The clock pin helps calibration where it is needed.**
- For `zcr-spsc-v3-2t`, 7 invocation pairs of 140 break their claim with the clock pinned, against 27 with it free.
- For `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` it is level, 11 against 9. That bench was already well calibrated.

**Two limits on this session.**
- My relaunch kept an ssh connection open for its first three minutes. I see no round-1 outlier in the cells I looked at, but I did not check all of them.
- The first launch left no records, so nothing from it is mixed in.

**What I take from all three sessions for the baseline config:**
- Pin the cpus by profile name and pin the clock.
- State the profile as part of what the baseline means.
- Expect the short settings to be enough for `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t`. We think `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` on `smt` needs more runs rather than longer ones.
- The run-length rung can test that directly. A retrospective subset of a 30-run invocation would show how the claim falls with `runs`, at no extra design cost.

The 7600X section is in `tmp/experiments/pins/README.md` with the full tables and the `pins.py` line that prints them.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# The pins experiment: what the cpu pin and the clock pin each buy, on this host.
#
# Every NAME=CPUS on the line is a cpu pin, and `none`, the unpinned case, is always one more.
# Each is crossed with the clock pin (pin, free), and each condition is an invocation of
# pins.toml with its pins on the line and a tag for each factor, `cpus=NAME` and
# `freq=pin|free`. The conditions go round-robin, the start rotating each round, so a drift over
# the run lands on every condition alike and none always follows the same neighbor. The script
# runs from its own directory, so the records land beside it, and the host is left alone until
# it ends.
#
#   ./pins.sh NAME=CPUS...
#   ./pins.sh hi=11,23 lo=0,12                         # the 3900X rows of records/pins.jsonl
#   ./pins.sh smt=11,23 ccx=11,10 x-ccx=11,8           # 3900X, every profile on the last core
#   ./pins.sh smt=5,11 ccx=5,4 lo-smt=0,6 lo-ccx=0,1   # 7600X
#
# ROUNDS is the invocations of each condition, 8 by default. FREQ is the clock conditions,
# "pin free" by default, so FREQ=pin halves the run once the clock pin is settled. BIN names the
# binary, iiac-perf-dev while a cycle runs. An invocation of the two benches is about 45 s, so the
# 7600X line above is 10 conditions by 8 rounds, about an hour.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
mkdir -p records # iiac-perf opens the record file and does not create its directory

rounds=${ROUNDS:-8}
bin=${BIN:-iiac-perf-dev}
read -r -a freqs <<<"${FREQ:-pin free}"

if (($# == 0)); then
    echo "usage: pins.sh NAME=CPUS..." >&2
    exit 2
fi

conditions=()
for pin in "$@" none=; do
    if [[ $pin != *=* ]]; then
        echo "error: '$pin' is not NAME=CPUS" >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    for freq in "${freqs[@]}"; do
        conditions+=("$pin $freq")
    done
done
n=${#conditions[@]}

for ((r = 0; r < rounds; r++)); do
    for ((i = 0; i < n; i++)); do
        read -r pin freq <<<"${conditions[(r + i) % n]}"
        name=${pin%%=*}
        cpus=${pin#*=}
        args=(pins.toml --tag "cpus=$name" --tag "freq=$freq")
        if [[ -n $cpus ]]; then
            args+=(--pin-cpus "$cpus")
        fi
        if [[ $freq == pin ]]; then
            args+=(--pin-freq)
        fi
        echo "== round $((r + 1))/$rounds: cpus=$name${cpus:+ ($cpus)} freq=$freq"
        "$bin" "${args[@]}"
    done
done

Splitting the smooth run into its own experiment is the right call. I found one naming inconsistency, one README line your move left stale, and material that belongs in `smooth/` but is not there yet.

**What you changed, as I read it**
- You created `tmp/experiments/smooth/` with a `README.md` and the screen capture, renamed to `smooth-screens-3900x-all-20260919T053912Z.out`.
- You removed `pins/screens/`, where I had put that capture.
- Nothing else under `tmp/experiments/` is newer than my last edits.

**Why the split is right**
- The smooth run asked a different question from the pins experiment: does the whole suite repeat at the short settings, day to day?
- The pins experiment took its hypotheses from it but shares no data with it.
- A directory per question is the layout we agreed for the new repo.

**Findings**
1. **The stamp is the end time, not the start.**
   - `053912Z` is the closing prompt in the capture (`05:39:12.209Z`). The run started at `05:29:24`.
   - The three pins sessions are stamped with their start (the first record's `t_start`), so the two experiments currently disagree.
   - I would use `20260919T052924Z`.
2. **The name has a slot the pins names lack.**
   - `…-3900x-all-…` puts the bench list between host and stamp.
   - That is fine as a pattern, `<experiment>-<kind>-<host>[-<what>]-<stamp>`, but the pins README should state it once so the next experiment follows it.
3. **`pins/README.md` line 24 is now wrong.** It says the capture "is under `screens/`", which no longer exists. It should point at `../smooth/`.
4. **The smooth README is missing what makes it an experiment record.**
   - It has the command and the impression, but not the following:
     - the date;
     - the binary version (0.28.17-4);
     - the fact that `record` was `none`, so the screen capture is the only copy of that run. That is the reason the file is a `.out` and not a `.jsonl`.

5. **The recorded rerun belongs here and is still in the repo's `tmp/`.**
   - `tmp/20260919T144009Z-4776-3900x.jsonl` is the same command run nine hours later with records: 280 of them, 28 benches.

- the pending pins edits.

# The smooth experiment

A run of every bench on the 3900X at short settings, the last core's SMT pair and the clock both
pinned, whose output was smooth and consistent, much different from what this host had shown
before (wink, 2026-09-19). The question it raised: do numbers this short repeat, and can their
error bars be believed? It is what the pins experiment, `../pins/`, took its hypotheses from.

## Recreating it

One line, from the iiac-perf checkout, under 0.28.17-4, the host left alone while it runs, about
10 minutes:

    iiac-perf-dev --benches=all --decimals 3 -d 0.250 --runs 10 --run-sleep 100ms --settle-time 0.1s --warm-cap 100ms --blocks 10 --block-sleep 100-200ms --pin-freq --pin-cpus 11,23

- The host's XDG config needs a `[freq]` table for `--pin-freq`, which `setup-freq` writes.
- A session's files are named `smooth-KIND-HOST-WHAT-STAMP`, the kind `records` or `screens`, the
  stamp the session's start in UTC.
- Sessions:
  - `smooth-screens-3900x-all-20260919T052924Z.out`: the first run, 05:29:24Z to 05:39:12Z by its
    own prompts. `record` was `none`, so this capture is the only copy, and its first four lines
    are the command, added above the terminal's text.
  - `smooth-records-3900x-all-20260919T144009Z.jsonl`: the same line nine hours later with
    `--record` and a tag, 280 records of 28 benches. The three probe benches record nothing.
- Numbers: `python3 cmp.py` compares the two sessions bench by bench, reading the first from its
  screen text, and `python3 outliers.py` lists the second's disturbed blocks. Both are throwaway
  and both hard-code the 10-50 trim for ten runs, until `iiac-perf analyze` can take their place.

## 3900X, 2026-09-19

- The trimmed mean repeats: 20 of 28 benches agree within 0.5% between the sessions and 16
  within 0.12%, `min-now` to 0.01% and `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` to 0.08%. The plain mean puts 14 of 28
  outside 0.5%.
- The claim does not always hold: 7 of 28 moved by more than sqrt(2) times the first session's
  `LSC trimmed`, where about 1 would if it were honest. They are `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` by 42 times,
  `zcr-spsc-v0-1t` 3.5, `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` 3.3, `std-now` 2.8, `ice-rr-1t` and `zcr-mpsc-v0-1t`
  1.4, and `mpsc-2t` 1.1.
- The worst is a bench on levels. `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` ran 6 runs near 16.98 ns and 4 near 19.15 in
  the first session, and 4, 5, and one at 22.99 in the second, so the four kept runs were all on
  one level the first time, a winsorized stdev of 0.003 ns, and straddled two the second.
- The second session's first 117 s held 22 blocks 30 to 37% over their run's median, about one
  every 5 s, across `min-now`, `std-now`, `mpsc-1t`, `mpsc-2t-spin`, and `probe-mpsc-2t`, and
  none from there to 450 s. The clock read 3.7676 GHz in those blocks as in every other, so it
  was not the frequency. We think it was the host still in use just after the launch.
- The block lag-1 averages -0.25 to +0.22 by bench, against +0.78 unpinned and +0.20 pinned on
  this host at a hundred blocks. Ten blocks make it a coarse estimate.

What it does not say: two sessions are one difference per bench, so a bench inside its claim may
have been lucky and one outside it unlucky, which is why the pins experiment ran 8 invocations a
cell.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# The pins experiment: what the cpu pin and the clock pin each buy, on this host.
#
# Every NAME=CPUS on the line is a cpu pin, and `none`, the unpinned case, is always one more.
# Each is crossed with the clock pin (pin, free), and each condition is an invocation of
# pins.toml with its pins on the line and a tag for each factor, `cpus=NAME` and
# `freq=pin|free`. The conditions go round-robin, the start rotating each round, so a drift over
# the run lands on every condition alike and none always follows the same neighbor. The script
# runs from its own directory, so the records land beside it, and the host is left alone until
# it ends.
#
#   ./pins.sh NAME=CPUS...
#   ./pins.sh hi=11,23 lo=0,12                         # the 3900X rows of records/pins.jsonl
#   ./pins.sh smt=11,23 ccx=11,10 x-ccx=11,8           # 3900X, every profile on the last core
#   ./pins.sh smt=5,11 ccx=5,4 lo-smt=0,6 lo-ccx=0,1   # 7600X
#
# ROUNDS is the invocations of each condition, 8 by default. FREQ is the clock conditions,
# "pin free" by default, so FREQ=pin halves the run once the clock pin is settled. BIN names the
# binary, iiac-perf-dev while a cycle runs. An invocation of the two benches is about 45 s, so the
# 7600X line above is 10 conditions by 8 rounds, about an hour.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
mkdir -p records # iiac-perf opens the record file and does not create its directory

rounds=${ROUNDS:-8}
bin=${BIN:-iiac-perf-dev}
read -r -a freqs <<<"${FREQ:-pin free}"

if (($# == 0)); then
    echo "usage: pins.sh NAME=CPUS..." >&2
    exit 2
fi

conditions=()
for pin in "$@" none=; do
    if [[ $pin != *=* ]]; then
        echo "error: '$pin' is not NAME=CPUS" >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    for freq in "${freqs[@]}"; do
        conditions+=("$pin $freq")
    done
done
n=${#conditions[@]}

for ((r = 0; r < rounds; r++)); do
    for ((i = 0; i < n; i++)); do
        read -r pin freq <<<"${conditions[(r + i) % n]}"
        name=${pin%%=*}
        cpus=${pin#*=}
        args=(pins.toml --tag "cpus=$name" --tag "freq=$freq")
        if [[ -n $cpus ]]; then
            args+=(--pin-cpus "$cpus")
        fi
        if [[ $freq == pin ]]; then
            args+=(--pin-freq)
        fi
        echo "== round $((r + 1))/$rounds: cpus=$name${cpus:+ ($cpus)} freq=$freq"
        "$bin" "${args[@]}"
    done
done

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Compare two smooth sessions bench by bench.

    python3 cmp.py A B

A and B are each a session's records file, `.jsonl`, or its screens file, `.out`, whose run rows
are read from the text. Throwaway, until `iiac-perf analyze` can: it hard-codes the 10-50 trim
and the `LSC trimmed` of src/series.rs for ten runs.
"""

import json
import math
import re
import statistics as st
import sys

T975_DF6 = 2.447  # t(0.975, 2 * kept - 2), kept = 4


def load(path):
    """bench -> run means, in the file's order."""
    runs = {}
    if path.endswith(".jsonl"):
        for line in open(path):
            try:
                r = json.loads(line)
            except json.JSONDecodeError:
                continue
            runs.setdefault(r["bench"], []).append(r["mean_ns"])
        return runs
    bench = None
    for line in open(path):
        m = re.match(r"^(\S+): 10 runs", line)
        if m:
            bench = m.group(1)
            runs[bench] = []
            continue
        m = re.match(r"^\s+\d+\s+\d+\s+([\d,.]+) ns", line)
        if m and bench:
            runs[bench].append(float(m.group(1).replace(",", "")))
    return {b: v for b, v in runs.items() if v}


def trimmed(v):
    s = sorted(v)
    return sum(s[1:5]) / 4


def lsc(v):
    s = sorted(v)
    w = [min(max(x, s[1]), s[4]) for x in v]
    return T975_DF6 * st.stdev(w) / (0.4 * math.sqrt(10)) * math.sqrt(2)


def main(a_path, b_path):
    a, b = load(a_path), load(b_path)
    print(f"{'bench':18}{'A trim':>10}{'B trim':>10}{'d%':>8}{'A plain':>10}{'B plain':>10}{'d%':>8}{'d/claim':>9}")
    inside = beyond = 0
    out = []
    for bench in a:
        if bench not in b or len(a[bench]) != 10 or len(b[bench]) != 10:
            continue
        ta, tb = trimmed(a[bench]), trimmed(b[bench])
        pa, pb = st.mean(a[bench]), st.mean(b[bench])
        claim = math.sqrt((lsc(a[bench]) ** 2 + lsc(b[bench]) ** 2) / 2)
        q = abs(ta - tb) / claim if claim else float("inf")
        inside += abs(tb / ta - 1) <= 0.005
        if q > 1:
            beyond += 1
            out.append(f"{bench} {q:.1f}x")
        print(f"{bench:18}{ta:10.3f}{tb:10.3f}{(tb / ta - 1) * 100:8.2f}{pa:10.3f}{pb:10.3f}{(pb / pa - 1) * 100:8.2f}{q:9.1f}")
    n = inside and sum(1 for x in a if x in b and len(a[x]) == 10 and len(b[x]) == 10)
    print(f"\ntrimmed means within 0.5%: {inside} of {n}")
    print(f"apart by more than the two sessions' LSC trimmed: {beyond} of {n}")
    print(", ".join(out))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    main(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Compare two smooth sessions bench by bench.

    python3 cmp.py A B

A and B are each a session's records file, `.jsonl`, or its screens file, `.out`, whose run rows
are read from the text. Throwaway, until `iiac-perf analyze` can: it hard-codes the 10-50 trim
and the `LSC trimmed` of src/series.rs for ten runs.
"""

import json
import math
import re
import statistics as st
import sys

T975_DF6 = 2.447  # t(0.975, 2 * kept - 2), kept = 4


def load(path):
    """bench -> run means, in the file's order."""
    runs = {}
    if path.endswith(".jsonl"):
        for line in open(path):
            try:
                r = json.loads(line)
            except json.JSONDecodeError:
                continue
            runs.setdefault(r["bench"], []).append(r["mean_ns"])
        return runs
    bench = None
    for line in open(path):
        m = re.match(r"^(\S+): 10 runs", line)
        if m:
            bench = m.group(1)
            runs[bench] = []
            continue
        m = re.match(r"^\s+\d+\s+\d+\s+([\d,.]+) ns", line)
        if m and bench:
            runs[bench].append(float(m.group(1).replace(",", "")))
    return {b: v for b, v in runs.items() if v}


def trimmed(v):
    s = sorted(v)
    return sum(s[1:5]) / 4


def lsc(v):
    s = sorted(v)
    w = [min(max(x, s[1]), s[4]) for x in v]
    return T975_DF6 * st.stdev(w) / (0.4 * math.sqrt(10)) * math.sqrt(2)


def main(a_path, b_path):
    a, b = load(a_path), load(b_path)
    print(f"{'bench':18}{'A trim':>10}{'B trim':>10}{'d%':>8}{'A plain':>10}{'B plain':>10}{'d%':>8}{'d/claim':>9}")
    inside = beyond = 0
    out = []
    for bench in a:
        if bench not in b or len(a[bench]) != 10 or len(b[bench]) != 10:
            continue
        ta, tb = trimmed(a[bench]), trimmed(b[bench])
        pa, pb = st.mean(a[bench]), st.mean(b[bench])
        claim = math.sqrt((lsc(a[bench]) ** 2 + lsc(b[bench]) ** 2) / 2)
        q = abs(ta - tb) / claim if claim else float("inf")
        inside += abs(tb / ta - 1) <= 0.005
        if q > 1:
            beyond += 1
            out.append(f"{bench} {q:.1f}x")
        print(f"{bench:18}{ta:10.3f}{tb:10.3f}{(tb / ta - 1) * 100:8.2f}{pa:10.3f}{pb:10.3f}{(pb / pa - 1) * 100:8.2f}{q:9.1f}")
    n = inside and sum(1 for x in a if x in b and len(a[x]) == 10 and len(b[x]) == 10)
    print(f"\ntrimmed means within 0.5%: {inside} of {n}")
    print(f"apart by more than the two sessions' LSC trimmed: {beyond} of {n}")
    print(", ".join(out))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    main(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])

content.text:
Yes, that is `d%`. `d/claim` is the same difference in nanoseconds, divided by a combined error bar built from both sessions:

```
d/claim = |A_trim - B_trim| / sqrt((LSC_A² + LSC_B²) / 2)
```

`LSC_A` and `LSC_B` are each session's own `LSC trimmed`. The script recomputes them from that session's ten run means with the formula in `src/series.rs`.

**The steps, for one session of ten runs:**
1. Sort the ten run means. The 10-50 trim keeps ranks 2 to 5, so the trimmed mean is the average of those four.
2. Winsorize: clamp every one of the ten values into the range from the 2nd to the 5th. The fastest run is pulled up to the 2nd value, and the five slowest are pulled down to the 5th.
3. Take the sample standard deviation of those ten clamped values. This is the report's `winsorized stdev`.
4. Standard error of the trimmed mean: `se = winsorized_stdev / (0.4 × sqrt(10))`. The 0.4 is the kept share, 4 of 10.
5. `LSC trimmed = t × se × sqrt(2)`, with `t = 2.447`, the 97.5% Student's t at 2×4−2 = 6 degrees of freedom.

**What `LSC` means.** It is the smallest difference between two trimmed means that you would call real at 95%, if both came from sessions with this spread. The `sqrt(2)` is there because a difference of two means has twice the variance of one mean.

**Why the two are combined as a root mean square.** Each `LSC` already assumes the other side is as noisy as itself. When the two sessions have different spreads, the right bar for their difference uses the average of the two variances, which is that RMS. If `LSC_A = LSC_B`, it reduces to the `LSC` itself.

**Reading it.**
- A value of 1.0 means the sessions differ by exactly the smallest change they claim to be able to detect.
- Below 1, the sessions agree within their claim.
- Above 1, they moved more than they said they could distinguish, so the claim was too tight. About 1 bench in 20 should land above 1 by chance if the claims are honest.

**A worked row, `cb-chan-2t`.**
- The trimmed means are 94.942 and 94.608 ns, so `|d|` = 0.334 ns.
- `d/claim` = 1.6 means the combined bar was about 0.21 ns, or about 0.22% of the mean.
- The two sessions moved 0.35% apart, so this row is flagged.

**Two things the number does not capture.**
- A big `d%` can hide behind a wide claim. `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` moved 2.36% and scores 0.2, because a session straddling two levels has a large winsorized stdev and therefore a large `LSC`. A low `d/claim` means the claim is honest, not that it is useful. Read `d/claim` together with how big the `LSC` is as a percent of the mean.
- It is only as good as ten runs. With four kept runs, the winsorized stdev is itself a noisy estimate. When the kept four happen to agree, `LSC` comes out tiny and a small real move scores high. The first session's `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` was that case, with a claim of 0.009 ns.

The plain version: `d/claim` asks whether the two sessions differ by more than their own error bars say they could tell apart. The error bar comes from how spread out each session's kept runs are, blended across the two sessions. Under 1 is consistent. Over 1 means the error bar was too optimistic.

If you want, I can add an `LSC%` column to `cmp.py` beside `d/claim`, as `pins.py` has. A wide-but-honest row like `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` would then show up in the table directly.

content.text:
The `LSC%` column is in. Your statement is nearly right, and it needs two qualifications.

**The goal as you put it**
- For any two runs of the same unmodified bench, the difference should be under `LSC`. That is calibration, and it is right in spirit.
- First, it is "about 19 times in 20", not "always".
  - `LSC` is a 95% threshold, so an honest config still lands over 1.0 on roughly 1 pair in 20 by chance.
  - A config that never exceeded its claim would be claiming too wide a bar.
  - The target is a rate near 5%, not zero.
  - The pins experiment counted exceedances out of 28 pairs for that reason. 0 to 2 is honest, and 9 is not.
- Second, that is only half the goal.
  - A wide bar passes that test trivially. `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` scores 0.2 because its claim is 12.58%.
  - The other half is that `LSC%` is small, since that is the smallest change you can detect.
  - The cycle's acceptance check puts that at 0.5%.

So the full goal for a baseline config, per bench, has two parts:
- `d/claim` stays under 1 for about 95% of pairs of unmodified runs. The bar is true.
- `LSC%` is at or under the change you want to be able to detect. The bar is useful.

When both hold, a modification that moves the trimmed mean by more than `LSC` is a real change, with about a 5% chance of a false alarm.

**The new column on the pair you ran**

| bench | d% | LSC% | d/claim | reading |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `min-now` | -0.02 | 0.04 | 0.6 | true and tight |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | -0.04 | 0.82 | 0.0 | true, a bit wide of 0.5% |
| `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` | 0.60 | 1.20 | 0.5 | true, too wide: a 1% change would be missed |
| `cb-chan-2t` | -0.35 | 0.23 | 1.6 | tight but broken here |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` | -2.36 | 12.58 | 0.2 | true and useless |

- The column splits the two ways a row can fail.
  - `cb-chan-2t` has a small claim that didn't hold.
  - `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` has a claim that held because it is enormous.
- Both of your target benches are honest but wider than 0.5% at these settings on the 3900X, at 0.82% and 1.20%. That matches what the pins experiment found.

**What one pair can and can't tell you**
- A single pair gives one draw per bench, so it can't measure the 5% rate.
- 28 benches give 28 draws, so 4 of 28 over 1.0 is mildly worse than the 1 or 2 expected.
- Most of those rows lean the same direction, so we think that is the slow session-to-session drift and not the claims being wrong within a session.
- Measuring the rate properly for one bench needs many sessions of that bench. The pins experiment ran 8 invocations per cell, and the unrun `claim/` experiment has 20.

The plain version: two unmodified runs should differ by less than the error bar most of the time, about 19 in 20, and the error bar also has to be small enough to be worth having. A bar that is never exceeded because it is huge tells you nothing. The new column shows the bar's size next to whether it held.

I also fixed a docstring line in `cmp.py` that my edit had left too long. The script output is unchanged: 21 of 28 within 0.5%, and 4 of 28 over their claim.

content.text:
I saw the move and updated `TODO.md` to match. I also read your new `smooth/config.toml`, and it has one problem.

**The move**
- `../iiac-perf-expr-1/` holds `claim/`, `pins/` and `smooth/`. Every file I had is there with its size unchanged, and `tmp/experiments/` no longer exists here.
- It is not a repo yet: it has no `.jj`, `.git` or `.vc-config.md`. It is still the only copy of about 27 MB of records. It is safer than `tmp/` was, but it is not under version control or backed up.

**`TODO.md`**
- The continuation notes and the `### An experiments repo` entry now name `../iiac-perf-expr-1`, credited to you and dated today. They say it is not yet under version control.
- `vc-x1 validate --fast` passes after the edit.

**`smooth/config.toml`**
- It reproduces the smooth command line as a config, which is the right idea. The values match the README's command: `all` benches, 0.25 s, 10 runs, 10 blocks, the same sleeps, `pin_cpus = "11,23"`, `pin_freq = "pin_mhz"`.
- The `record = "smooth-records"` line will not give you per-session files.
  - The path has no trailing `/`, so `iiac-perf` treats it as one file named `smooth-records`.
  - Every session would append to that one file, which is the combined-file layout we just split apart.
  - A trailing `/` makes it a directory, with one file per invocation named by series and host.
  - Neither form produces a `smooth-records-HOST-all-STAMP.jsonl` name.
- That session name has to be given on the command line, as `pins.sh` now does with `--record`. For smooth that needs a two-line wrapper script, or renaming the file after each run as you did yesterday.
- A smaller point: the file omits `block_warmup`.
  - Yesterday's runs got `2ms` from the project-local file, because they started inside this repo.
  - Started from `../iiac-perf-expr-1/smooth/`, no project-local file is found, so the built-in default applies, which the template shows as `0`.
  - A session recorded from the new location would then not match the three already there. Adding `block_warmup = "2ms"` makes the file self-contained.
- I have not changed the file. Say the word and I'll add the wrapper script and the `block_warmup` line.

**Still open in this repo**
- The rung `chore: host facts leave the project configs` is at its work review, unpushed, and waiting on your "continue".

content.text:
`iiac-perf` can't produce that name by itself today. I also described the no-slash form badly yesterday, so here are both forms again.

**Directory form**
- A record path ending in `/` is a directory.
- The tool names the file itself as `<series>-<host>.jsonl`. The series is the UTC start plus the parent process id, and the pid is your five digits.
- I checked `src/record.rs`: the format is fixed at `"{}-{}.jsonl"`, with no template or prefix option.
- So `20260920T171448Z-38039-3900x.jsonl` is the only shape that form produces.

**File form**
- A record path without a trailing `/` is taken as one literal file name, used exactly as written.
- Nothing is substituted into it. `record = "smooth-records"` appends every session to a single file literally named `smooth-records`, which is not what you want.

**How to get the name you want today**
- The exact name needs a stamp, and only the shell can supply it. Pass the full name on the command line:

```
iiac-perf-dev --config config.toml --record "smooth-records-$(uname -n)-all-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).jsonl"
```

- `--record` on the line overrides the file's `record` key. `pins.sh` does the same thing for its experiment.
- For your one-bench run the middle part would be `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` in place of `all`. You have to type that part, because the shell doesn't know which benches ran.
- A two-line wrapper script in `smooth/` would save the typing. It would also capture the screen output to the matching `smooth-screens-…out`. Say so and I'll write it.

**Whether the tool's own name is good enough**
- The tool's name and yours carry almost the same information.

| | tool's name | your name |
|---|---|---|
| start | `20260920T171448Z` | `STAMP` |
| host | `3900x` | `HOST` |
| uniqueness | pid `38039` | none |
| experiment | the directory, `smooth-records/` | `smooth-records-` prefix |
| what ran | not in the name | `all` |

- The tool's form needs no wrapper.
  - It can't collide when two sessions start in the same second.
  - It sorts by time.
- What it lacks is the "what ran" part. Each record already carries that in its `bench` field and `tags`, so it is recoverable, just not visible in `ls`.
- The cost is that yesterday's sessions would be named differently from new ones unless I rename them to match.

**A third option, for later**
- If the prefixed name matters to you, the clean fix is in the tool. For example, a directory target could take a prefix, so `record = "smooth-records-/"` or a `record_prefix` key would give `smooth-records-<series>-<host>.jsonl`.
- That is a small feature and a Todo entry, not something to slip into the current rung.

I recommend the tool's directory form as it is, plus a `--tag what=all` (or `what=zcr-mpsc-v2-2t`) on the line when you want the run's scope recorded. That gives you zero scripts, unique names, and the scope in the data where `analyze` can read it. If you would rather have the scope visible in the file name, the one-line `--record` above does it today.

Your run is a fourth data point for that bench on `11,23` pinned:

| run | `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` trimmed mean | `LSC trimmed` |
|---|---|---|
| today | 64.264 ns | 0.353 ns (0.55%) |
| yesterday's smooth session | 63.962 ns | |
| yesterday's smooth session | 64.344 ns | |
| pins session | 65.337 ns | |

The pins figure is about 1.6% above the other three, more than any single session's claim allows. That is the session-to-session spread again, and it is the argument for alternating A and B within one session.

content.text:
The parent process creates `<series>` once, when the invocation starts, as the UTC time to the second followed by its own process id.

**Where it is made**
- `record::new_series_id()` in `src/record.rs` builds it as `"{stamp}-{pid}"`, where the stamp is `SystemTime::now()` in basic UTC form (`20260920T171448Z`) and the pid is `std::process::id()`.
- The doc comment there says why: "the UTC start to the second and the parent's pid, unique on a host and sorting in time order."
- `src/main.rs` line 1695 calls it once per invocation while building the `RecordSpec`, before any bench runs.

**How it reaches the file name**
- Every run of every bench is a fresh child process. The parent gives each child the same `RecordSpec`, series id included, and the child stamps it on its records (`recorder.set_series` in `src/child.rs`).
- With a directory target, each child computes the file name itself, as `<series>-<host>.jsonl`.
  - All children share one series id, so they all compute the same name and append to the same file.
  - That is how ten runs of 28 benches, 280 separate processes, end up in one file without coordinating.

**Reading your example**
- Your file is `20260920T171448Z-38039-3900x.jsonl`.
  - `20260920T171448Z` is when the parent started, 17:14:48 UTC.
  - `38039` is the parent's pid.
  - `3900x` is the host name.
- In your paste the run rows show pids 38050, 38053 and so on. Those are the children, all higher than the parent's 38039.
- The shell prompt reads 17:14:41 and the stamp reads 17:14:48, seven seconds later. That is the same gap you worked out by hand yesterday between the prompt time and the real start.

**Two consequences**
- The stamp is the invocation's start, not any one run's.
  - Each record carries its own `t_start`, plus the shared `series` and its `run` number, in the data.
  - That is why I could split yesterday's combined pins file back into sessions.
- The pid is there for uniqueness.
  - The stamp alone is to the second, and two invocations started in the same second on one host would otherwise collide.
  - A name like `smooth-records-HOST-all-STAMP.jsonl` gives that up, which is a small risk for something you start by hand.

**Series versus session**
- A series is one invocation of `iiac-perf`.
- Your smooth sessions are one invocation each, so series and session are the same thing there.
- A pins session is 48 to 96 invocations and so that many series.
  - That is why `pins.sh` names one file per session from the shell.
  - The tool's per-invocation naming would have produced up to 96 small files per pins session.

Two of the three already exist under other names. The third is a real gap, and I'd fill it slightly differently from how you put it.

**`--id <value>`: this is `--tag` today**
- `--tag id=baseline` puts `"tags": {"id": "baseline"}` on every record of that invocation.
- The pins experiment ran on exactly this: `cpus=smt` and `freq=pin` were the keys `pins.py` grouped and compared by.
- The missing piece is on the reading side, not the recording side. `analyze` should take the tag to compare by, something like `analyze FILE --by id`. That gives "baseline against modification" directly, which is your actual goal.
- A free-form tag is more flexible than one fixed `--id`.
  - It allows two factors at once, as pins needed.
  - Any key will do.
- One reason to name a key anyway is a convention that `analyze` groups by `id` when told nothing else. That would be a default, not a new flag.

**`--append <file>`: this is `--record FILE` without the trailing slash**
- A `--record` path with no slash is one literal file that every run appends to. `pins.sh` builds a whole session into one file that way.
- Your instinct is still pointing at a real defect. The mode is encoded in a trailing `/`, which is invisible and bit both of us yesterday.
  - Your `record = "smooth-records"` would have quietly appended everything to one oddly named file.
- The fix is to make the intent explicit, either as two spellings like `--record-file PATH` and `--record-dir DIR`, or by keeping `--record` and having the banner say which mode it took.
  - For example `record smooth-records/ (a directory, one file per invocation)`.
- I lean toward the banner line as the cheap step and the two spellings as the clean one.

**`--fname-tag`: the real gap, but I would not let the user define the series**
- The series id does two jobs.
  - It names the file.
  - It is also written into every record as the identity of the invocation.
- The series id is how 280 child processes agree on one file without coordinating. It is also how `analyze` knows which ten runs form one invocation, so that a trimmed mean and its `LSC` are computed over the right ten.
- If a user supplied the series and reused a value, two invocations would merge into one "invocation" of twenty runs. The statistics would then be silently wrong.
- So I would keep the series automatic and unique and add a label beside it.
  - A `--record-label smooth-all` would give `smooth-all-20260920T171448Z-38039-3900x.jsonl` in the directory form.
  - That is your naming scheme with the pid kept for uniqueness.
  - The label would go into the record as well, so the file name never knows something the data doesn't.
- That is a small, contained change: one optional string in `RecordSpec`, used in the one `format!` that builds the name.

**How the three fit together for your goal**

```
iiac-perf-dev --config baseline.toml --record runs/ --record-label ring-ab --tag id=base
iiac-perf-dev --config baseline.toml --record runs/ --record-label ring-ab --tag id=mod
iiac-perf-dev analyze runs/ --by id
```

- These are two invocations, alternated as many times as you like.
- Each gets a uniquely named file.
- `analyze` reads the directory and reports `base` against `mod` with the claim for each.
- The Todo `### Analyze a directory of records` already plans the directory reading.

I would cross-link it to `### Compare two builds in one invocation`. Separately, the record-directory creation bug from the 7600X launch is still not recorded anywhere.

content.text:
**The units.** There are three levels, and every question `analyze` can answer is about one of them.
- A run is one process and gives one mean.
- An invocation is a series of ten runs. It gives a trimmed mean and its own `LSC trimmed`.
- A group is several invocations of the same thing, selected by a tag or by the bench name.

The third level is where yesterday's findings came from. One invocation can state a claim, but only a group can check it.

**1. Qualifying a baseline: A against A.** This is your "ideally identical" set, and I'd make it the first thing `analyze` does.
- It reports four things for the group:
  - How far apart the invocations' trimmed means sit.
  - How that spread compares with the claimed `LSC`.
  - How many pairs exceed their claim.
  - Whether the means trend with session order, which is the drift we saw.
- It also reports an "effective" smallest detectable change, built from the spread between invocations and not from inside one invocation.
  - The within-invocation claim can't see drift.
  - The between-invocation spread includes it, so it is the honest number for "would I notice a 0.5% change?".
  - For `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` on the 7600X the two numbers agreed.
  - For the 3900X `ccx` cell they didn't.

**2. A against B.** Two groups, the same bench under two builds or two settings, told apart by a tag.
- Pooling each side and comparing the two means is the weak form.
- If the invocations alternate A, B, A, B, the strong form pairs each A with its neighbouring B and analyses the differences.
  - A slow drift moves both members of a pair together and cancels.
  - The error bar then comes from how much the differences vary, which is usually much tighter.
- The output is the change in percent with its interval and a plain verdict:
  - detected,
  - not detected,
  - or "not detected, and this design could only have seen changes above X%".
- The third verdict matters most to you. It separates "no change" from "couldn't tell".

**3. A ladder, `zcr-spsc-v{n}-2t`.** This is a different shape, and in one way an easier one.
- The versions are different bench names in the same binary, so one invocation can run all of them.
  - No tag is needed, because the bench name is the factor.
  - Each invocation yields every version under the same host state a few seconds apart.
  - So the versions are paired across the ladder for free.
- Two comparisons are worth printing:
  - Each version against the first, the total gain.
  - Each version against the one before, the gain of that step.
- I would not print all pairs. Every comparison carries about a 5% false-alarm rate, so with five versions an all-pairs table has ten chances to mislead. The two comparisons above match how you think about a ladder.
- The caveat is that a version's own level structure can swamp its step. `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` moves 12% between its own levels, so a 3% step over v2 is invisible there. The ladder view should show each version's effective detectable change beside its step, so a step smaller than its bar reads as "unknown".

**4. A grid of conditions.** This is the pins shape: two tags crossed, a table of cells. It is the A-against-A report per cell plus comparisons along one tag while the other is held fixed. It needs nothing new beyond being able to name more than one tag.

**What cuts across all four.**
- The same per-group row serves every mode:
  - invocations,
  - trimmed mean,
  - between-invocation spread,
  - claimed `LSC`,
  - exceed rate,
  - drift.
- The modes differ only in which groups get compared and whether the comparison is paired.
- Pairing needs an order, and the records already carry `t_start` and the series, so alternation can be detected and not just assumed.
- Layout luck is the one confounder `analyze` can't fix for an A-against-B across two builds.
  - A code change moves where things land in memory, and that alone can shift a bench's level.
  - A real 1% "improvement" could be layout luck.
  - The Todos `### Replicate builds so layout is not confounded` and `### Measure whether code layout moves the level` are where that belongs.
  - It argues for treating a small A/B result as provisional until the change survives a rebuild.
- The rung text already keeps level clustering out of `analyze`, and I'd hold to that. `analyze` reports a wide bar honestly, and explaining the levels is separate work.

The plain version: `analyze` should first tell you whether a baseline is good enough to detect the size of change you care about. Then it should compare A with B using neighbouring pairs so slow drift cancels. For a ladder of versions it should run them all in the same invocation and report each step and the total, saying "can't tell" when a step is smaller than the noise.

On "let's try it": I want to be sure what you mean before I touch code, since the current rung is still at its work review. The three ideas are `--record-label`, an explicit record mode, and `analyze --by TAG`.
- The first two are small changes to recording.
- The third is the `analyze` rung itself, which is next in the ladder.

My suggestion is to finish the review of `chore: host facts leave the project configs` and push it. Then the recording changes go in as an inserted rung ahead of `analyze`, and `analyze` is built with `--by` from the start, along the four modes above. Is that the order you want, or did you mean something smaller by "try it", such as just recording the Todo?

Yes to both. If you had run `init-config` before moving, the new file would have inherited `block_warmup`, and a record is a good source of truth for a config, with two limits.

**Would `init-config` inside the repo have picked up `block_warmup`?**
- Yes. `init-config` starts from "the run keys this host's config files set", layered the way a run layers them, with the flags on the line applied on top.
- Yesterday's output shows it: `init-config: from iiac-perf.md: block_sleep, block_warmup, blocks`.
- Your smooth line overrides `blocks` and `block_sleep`, but not `block_warmup`, so `2ms` would have come through.
- The same layering also caused trouble yesterday. It is how the 3900X's `[freq]` ended up in a file named for the 7600X.
- The real hole is that a config file is one layer of what ran. It can't show what the other layers contributed.

**A record as the source of truth**
- A record is the only complete account of a run. Its `config.params` holds every key after all layers resolved, each with its value, where it came from, and whether it equals the default.
- I checked today's smooth record. It has `block_warmup` = `2 ms` sourced from your `config.toml`, `duration` = `250 ms`, `blocks` = `10`, and the rest.
- Most values already read back as config. I fed `duration = "250 ms"` and `block_sleep = "100-200 ms"` to the loader and it accepted both.
- So `init-config --from-record FILE` is mostly a matter of writing those values out.

**Limit 1: two keys are recorded for a reader, not for the loader**
- `pin_freq` reads `3801 MHz (base clock from acpi_cppc/nominal_freq)` and `freq` is a one-line summary. Neither parses back.
- The clean fix is for the record to carry the effective run config in loadable form alongside the readable one.
- That is a schema bump. The label idea also adds a record field, so I'd make both changes in the same rung under one bump.

**Limit 2: some of a record is the other host's facts and must not transfer**
- For your "someone gave me a run" case, this limit is the point.
- `[freq]` is theirs. Their clamp is wrong on your host, which is the same bug as yesterday.
- `pin_freq` as a number is theirs too. If their record says the source was the word `pin_mhz`, the new config should carry the word so it resolves to your host's clock.
- `pin_cpus = "11,23"` is their topology.
  - The record has the cpu numbers and a `host.caches` block, but no placement label.
  - The banner prints `at 11,23 SMT`, but I found no such field in the record.
  - Without the label, a tool can't know that `11,23` there should become `5,11` here. The record should carry it.
- `record` and the file paths are theirs as well.
- So the generated config is the run keys, plus host facts translated where the record says enough, and left out with a comment where it doesn't.

**What "duplicate as best as possible" can honestly mean**
- The same config is not the same run. The record also names the cpu model, kernel, rustc, and `iiac-perf` version.
- The useful companion to the config is a short report of where you differ, for example: "their cpu is X, yours is Y, their version is 0.28.17-4, yours is -5".
- That is what stops you reading a host difference as a bench difference.
- The record does not carry the bench source's commit, only the tool's version. For reproducing someone else's run that may be the most important missing field.

**A cheaper half that would have caught your `block_warmup` case**
- A comparison should check that the two sides ran the same config, and say so when they didn't.
- `analyze` has both records' `config.params` in hand, so that is a few lines of code.
- A session recorded from the new directory without `block_warmup` would then have been flagged when compared with yesterday's, instead of looking like a small shift in the bench.

**Where it goes**
- I'd add it to the recording rung that goes in ahead of `analyze`. That rung would hold the label, the explicit record mode, the loadable config and placement label in the record, and `init-config --from-record`.
- `analyze` then gets the config check along with `--by`.
- If that makes the recording rung too big, `--from-record` splits off cleanly as its own rung. It only reads what the first rung adds.

The plain version: a config file only shows part of what ran, but a record shows all of it, so building a config from a record is sound. It needs two small additions to what the record stores, and it must leave the other machine's clock and cpu numbers behind. Comparisons should also warn when the two sides didn't use the same settings.

The order is still your pick. The rung `chore: host facts leave the project configs` is at its work review. Say "continue" when the diff looks right and I'll write its description. The recording rung comes after it, and I'll write its plan into the ladder at that point and nothing before.

message.content: I'm feeling the current change is somewhat related to creating the 7600x configs. Seems we need the notion of a "hosts" configuration which is separate from a projects configuration. So instead of one config file, it seems we need at least two, maybe three. One for the host, one for project has a whole and a third for analyzing.

content.text:
The host/project split is right, and the tool is already about two-thirds of the way there: the files exist, but nothing enforces the boundary between them. I'd add the third, analysis file later, for a different reason.

**What exists today.**
- A host file, the XDG config.
- A project file, `iiac-perf.toml`, found up the parent directories.
- A named run config, such as `configs/claim.toml` or your `smooth/config.toml`.
- They differ only by location. Any of them may hold any key.
  - That is how the 3900X's `[freq]` clamp got into a file named for the 7600X.
  - It is also how `block_warmup` silently depended on which directory you stood in.
- The docs even bless this. They say a project-local `[freq]` "replaces the XDG one whole."

**What you're describing is a split by kind of key, and enforced.**

| file | holds | property |
|---|---|---|
| host | `[freq]` and `[profiles]` now; later the measured values, such as a host's `pin_mhz` and settle time | true of one machine, wrong on any other |
| project / run | benches, duration, runs, blocks, sleeps, `pin_cpus = "smt"`, `pin_freq = "pin_mhz"`, record, tags | names host facts and never states them, so it runs unedited anywhere |
| analysis | what to group and compare by, pairing, the trim band, the target `LSC%`, which ladder comparisons | describes reading the records, not producing them |

- The run config refers to the host only through names: a profile name and a clock word.
  - That is the whole reason the same file worked on both hosts yesterday.
- Enforcing it would mean that a `[freq]` or `[profiles]` table outside the host file is an error, or at least a loud warning.
  - A documented override would be the escape hatch, since "this benchmark directory holds its own clock" is a real use.
  - With that rule, yesterday's bug becomes impossible instead of something to remember.
- It also settles the record-to-config idea.
  - A record's run keys go into a run config.
  - Its host block is compared against your host file.
  - Nothing of theirs lands in yours.

**On the analysis file, a caution.**
- The case for it is that a reproducible analysis needs its choices written down, just as a run does.
  - Your experiment READMEs already feel that need.
  - Each has a "Numbers:" line that would become `analyze --config pins-analysis.toml`.
- One key is already misfiled.
  - `trim_runs` lives in the run config, but it changes nothing about how a run executes. It only changes how run means are summarized afterwards.
  - The template's own text says it is "set once for a project, never per comparison", which describes an analysis setting.
- The case against it is that `analyze` doesn't exist yet.
  - Designing a config format for an unbuilt tool means guessing its knobs.
  - I'd build `analyze` with flags, see which ones every experiment ends up passing, and promote those to a file once they hold still.
  - The `trim_runs` question can wait for the same moment.

**How this relates to the work in flight.**
- Your feeling that the current rung belongs to this is right. It is even titled for it: `chore: host facts leave the project configs`.
- That rung is the data half of the idea.
  - The tables came out of the project file and the two 7600X configs.
  - The host files were built as the home for `[freq]` and `[profiles]`.
- The rung does not enforce anything.
- So I'd keep the rung as it is and let the idea shape what comes after:
  - The `setup-host` Todo gains the enforcement: the loader refuses host tables outside the host file.
  - The recording rung's `--from-record` translates through the host file.
  - The analysis config waits until `analyze` has taught us its knobs.

The plain version: the tool already has a host file and a project file. It just lets anything go in either, and that is what bit us. The fix is to make machine facts legal only in the host file and have every other config refer to them by name. A third file for analysis choices makes sense, but it should come after the analysis tool exists, so it records real choices instead of guesses.

There is one thing I'd do now if you agree. The cycle-record's deliberation should carry this decision under your name, since it is the reason this rung exists and it shapes three later pieces of work. That is a few lines in `TODO.md`, inside the rung still at its work review. Shall I add it?

1577:## Bugs
### Compare two builds in one invocation

An A/B today is two invocations, and the same binary measured twice, clock pinned, differs by more
than its own `LSC runs`: 383.7 against 387.0 ns on the 3900X 90 minutes apart, and 70.0, 70.4, and
70.6 ns on the 7600x (wink, 2026-09-15, in `feat: CI95 and LSC across processes`, the A/A evidence
in [measuring-a-technique.md](notes/measuring-a-technique.md)). A pair measured in one invocation
with the arms alternating cancels whatever drifts between invocations.

- an arm is a binary and its knobs, so `--against PATH` running that binary's children alternately
  with this one's is the small version, and a config with two arms the general one
- the statistic is the paired difference or ratio and its interval, not two independent means: the
  pairing is what removes the invocation's own offset
- the ratio is what a claim about a technique carries between hosts, so this is the surface a
  cross-host table is built from
- it needs the run's arm in the record beside its `series` and `run`

### Replicate builds so layout is not confounded
### Analyze a directory of records

A record exists so a re-analysis can happen without the session that produced it, and nothing reads
one back, so every analysis is a throwaway script whose numbers nobody can check (wink, 2026-09-03,
reading the 7600X duration sweep). An `analyze` subcommand over a directory of records, sharing
`record.rs`'s struct so the schema keeps one owner.

- three tiers, in increasing order of what they are worth:
  - **tabulate**: pivot the records into a table on an axis, duration, host, bench, or run. The
    least interesting tier, and the one the other two are built on
  - **read the series nothing reads**: `block_mean_ns`, `block_samples`, `clock_t_ns`, `clock_cpu`,
    and `clock_khz` sit in every record and nothing reads them back, roughly a third of the file's
    bytes as dead weight. The drift and step signals are computed at run time and thrown away, and
    the record holds the raw material to recompute them
  - **make a cross-run claim**: the tool cannot make one at all today. Every number it prints is a
    within-invocation claim, and the guide already says so, treating `LSC` as a lower bound and
    telling the reader to run 3-5 interleaved and compare the per-run values by hand ([Comparing
    two implementations](docs/report-guide.md#comparing-two-implementations)). Nothing performs
    that comparison
- the cross-run tier is the entry's point: run-to-run scatter, a confidence interval on the mean of
  run means, and an `LSC` that is not fiction. Single-run resolution understates the real spread
  badly on the contended benches, `cb-chan-2t`'s 5 s and 30 s runs disagreeing by 10.9% while the
  5 s run claims 0.15% resolution, 64x its own claim
- one run per cell cannot say which of the two runs was the off one, so the sweep that found this
  was the wrong shape. 3-5 runs per cell, interleaved, is what the guide has said all along
- the output reuses the report's row names, so the guide decodes the new surface for free. Grading
  the set the way a run grades itself is the natural extension: do these runs agree, and is a
  disagreement drift, a step, or one bad run
- `--format csv` / `--format json` for the plotting hand-off, kin to "Machine-readable report
  output" below, one flag family
- its cross-run arithmetic is `feat: CI95 and LSC across processes`'s, one statistics module
  serving both, and the records carry the host block cross-host analysis needs, a hostname alone
  naming nothing

### A --pin-idle knob, forbidding deep C-states
## Bugs

_See [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md)._

## Closed

Definitions and Core Organization

* CCX (Core Complex): A group of CPU cores that directly share a local Last-Level L3 cache. In early
AMD Zen designs, a CCX maxed out at 4 cores and a dedicated 16MB L3 cache slice.

* CCD (Core Complex Die): The physical building block or chiplet on the CPU package that houses the
processing cores and their cache hierarchy.

Evolution of Cache and Die Layout (Zen to Zen 5)

* Zen / Zen 2: Each CCD contains two separate CCXs. For example, in Zen 2,
a single 8-core CCD is split into two 4-core CCXs, each with its own isolated 16MB L3 cache.
Cores on one CCX had to communicate with the other CCX via Infinity Fabric cross-talk, adding
latency.

Zen 3 through Zen 5: AMD merged the design so that each CCD contains a single CCX holding upi
to 8 cores. All 8 cores now share a single, unified 32MB L3 cache pool directly on the die,
which significantly lowers memory and cache latency.

Zen 4c (Compact): Reverts to a dual-CCX layout per CCD, packing 16 smaller dense cores split
into two 8-core CCXs to maximize efficiency and core count in a compact footprint.

content.text:
Both answered. You weren't asleep on the first one, and on the second you've caught a real error of mine.

## The `xdg-HOST` files

They're candidate replacements for each host's `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md`, built yesterday and never installed. They exist only in `tmp/`, which is ignored, so nothing you ran has used them.

```
[profiles]                      [profiles]
ccx   = "11,10"                 ccx = "5,4"
smt   = "11,23"                 smt = "5,11"
x-ccx = "11,8"                  [freq]
[freq]                          boost = true
boost = true                    epp = "balance_performance"
epp = "balance_performance"     governor = "powersave"
governor = "powersave"          max_mhz = 5457
max_mhz = 4673                  min_mhz = 2991
min_mhz = 1745                  pin_mhz = 4701
  (3900x)                         (7600x)
```

- They are exactly the host files we've been discussing: `[freq]` plus `[profiles]`, nothing else, in the slim TOML form.
- The `[freq]` tables are each host's real values. The 7600X's I read off that host's live `config.md` over ssh, and they match.
- The 3900X's file keeps the `# pin_mhz omitted: the base clock` comment, so it behaves as today.
- `~/.config/iiac-perf/` still holds only `config.md` on both hosts. Installing means copying the file in and moving `config.md` aside, since both present is a hard error.
- `configs/claim.toml` can't run until the 3900X one is installed, because it says `pin_cpus = "smt"` and nothing defines `smt` yet.

## CCX and CCD: you're right, and I conflated two different hops

Your Google answer matches this host exactly. The 3900X is Zen 2: 12 cores, four L3 groups of three (16 MB each, one core disabled per four-core CCX), two CCXs per CCD.

That gives **four** placements from base core 11, not three:

| profile | cpus | what it crosses | measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| `smt` | 11,23 | nothing, two threads of one core | 61-65 ns |
| `ccx` | 11,10 | a core, same L3 | 122-123 ns |
| `x-ccx` | 11,8 | an L3, **same CCD** (groups 2,3 are both CCD 1) | 367-397 ns |
| `x-ccd` | 11,5 | a die (group 1 is CCD 0) | never run |

My error was on 2026-09-19, when I wrote that `ccd` should go and `x-ccx` was "what can be derived". The template's `ccd = "0,6"` genuinely crosses the dies: core 0 is CCD 0, core 6 is CCD 1. I replaced it with `11,8`, which does not. I treated a rename as if it were the same measurement, and it isn't.

**What I had right:** the kernel really can't see the CCD here. I just checked: `die_id` reads 0 on every cpu and `cluster_id` is 65535, unset. Only the L3 grouping is visible. So a `ccd` profile would come from knowing that Zen 2 lays groups 0-1 on one die and 2-3 on the other, which is architecture knowledge and a guess on the next machine. That is a reason for `setup-host` to be careful, not a reason the hop doesn't exist.

**What's worth measuring.** On Zen 2 all CCX-to-CCX traffic goes through the I/O die, so I'd expect `x-ccd` to land near `x-ccx`'s 367-397 ns rather than higher. That's from memory and it is testable with the tool we have:

```
./pins.sh ccx=11,10 x-ccx=11,8 x-ccd=11,5
```

Six conditions, about 48 minutes. If `x-ccd` matches `x-ccx`, one profile covers both on Zen 2 and the name should say "crosses an L3". If it's higher, they're distinct and the 3900X needs all four.

**One naming question this raises,** for the placements Todo that fixes the built-in names: `ccx` and `ccd` are AMD's words for things the kernel reports as L3 sharing. On Zen 3+ one CCX is one CCD, so `x-ccx` and `x-ccd` mean the same pair, and on Intel an L3 spans the socket and neither exists. Whether the built-in names should be AMD's or should say what sysfs sees is your call, and I haven't recorded a position.

**Fixed in `TODO.md`:** the `setup-host` entry's `ccd` line now says it's a fourth placement and not a rename, marks it as my error corrected, gives the `11,5` pair, states what sysfs does and doesn't expose, and notes the cost is unmeasured. `vc-x1 validate --fast` passes.

content.text:
Right, and `pins.toml` already isn't "all" — it runs only `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` and `zcr-spsc-v3-2t`. The `all` bench list belongs to the smooth experiment.

I also miscounted in my last message: `./pins.sh ccx=... x-ccx=... x-ccd=...` is 8 conditions, not 6, because `pins.sh` always adds `none` and crosses everything with pinned and free.

**The full design is overkill here.** Eight rounds exist to measure calibration — whether a claim holds across invocations — and that needs many invocations. The CCX/CCD question is a size question: is the cross-die hop near 390 ns or near 600? Within one invocation the claim is already 0.2 to 0.5%, so two or three invocations settle it.

```
FREQ=pin ROUNDS=3 ./pins.sh ccx=11,10 x-ccx=11,8 x-ccd=11,5
```

That's 4 conditions by 3 rounds, 12 invocations, about 9 minutes. `FREQ=pin` drops the free-clock half, which we already know buys nothing here, and `ccx` comes along to give the scale.

The one case needing more precision is if the two hops come out equal, since "they're the same" is a claim about a small difference and the session drift is 0.1 to 0.9%. Running `x-ccx` and `x-ccd` in the same session, as above, is what handles that.

**The larger point: this doesn't need doing now at all.** It buys nothing for the baseline config, which will name `smt` or `ccx`. It only matters for the built-in profile names, so it belongs with `### Placements by name and a cpus command` and can run whenever that comes up. I've left it in the `setup-host` Todo as unmeasured, with the pair to use.

content.text:
Conceding the first half and pushing back on the second.

**For the topology probe, one is enough.** We're asking whether a cross-die hop costs 390 ns or 600. That's a 3x question against a within-invocation claim of 0.06%. A second bench adds nothing. Use `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t`: its `x-ccx` cell was the tightest of the whole 3900X session at 0.060% spread. That halves it to about 4.5 minutes.

**For a pins session proper, two earned their keep, and I can show where.** On the 7600X, same host, same profile, same settings, clock pinned:

| bench | cpus | spread | claim |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` | smt | 0.089% | 0.185% |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | smt | 0.594% | 2.105% |

An 11-fold difference in the claim between two benches that differ only in which ring they exercise. With `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` alone we'd have concluded "the short settings on `smt` are three times better than the 0.5% target". With `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` alone, "`smt` is unusable, use `ccx`". Both would have been wrong as stated, and neither would have been detectably wrong.

The same thing happened with the drift. On the 3900X `ccx` cell, `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` broke its claim 7 times in 28 and `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` 0 times. One bench would have made that either a host problem or no problem.

So the jump from one to two is qualitative: it's the difference between reading an answer and learning that the answer depends on the bench. You can't get that from n=1 at any level of care.

**Why not 10.** The returns collapse right after that.
- One to two buys the existence of bench-dependence.
- Two to ten buys its distribution, which is a much smaller thing to want here.

Meanwhile the cost is linear and the harm is worse than linear. The 7600X session was 80 invocations in 54 minutes. At ten benches it would be about five hours, and its records would go from 7.7 MB to nearly 40. A five-hour session is also a worse experiment: the drift we're trying to average out is 0.1 to 0.9% between sessions, and more of it happens inside a session that long. The round-robin spreads it, but there is more of it to spread.

The decisive reason, though, is that the all-benches question already has an experiment. `smooth` runs all 28 in about ten minutes. That's where "which benches are well-behaved" gets answered, roughly 30 times cheaper per bench than pins could. The two experiments divide the work:

- `smooth`: every bench, few sessions, so you learn which benches misbehave.
- `pins`: few benches, many invocations, so you learn which setup misbehaves.

Ten benches in pins would be pins doing smooth's job badly.

**One thing I'd change.** Our two are the two rings you happen to be optimizing. That they bracket the behaviour so well was luck. If a pins session is being designed rather than inherited, the two should be picked to bracket deliberately: one bench known to be well-behaved and one known to be awkward, which `smooth` can now tell us. I haven't written that down — say the word and it goes in the `pins` README as a note on choosing benches.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Rank every bench of a smooth session by the width of the claim it makes about itself.

    python3 rank.py RECORDS... [--sort mean|worst]

Each bench gets its `LSC trimmed` as a percent of its trimmed mean, per session, and the rows
sort by the mean of those. The narrow end is where a baseline config can detect a small change;
the wide end is where it cannot, whether or not the claim is true. Which experiment a bench
belongs in is read off this, `pins` wanting one bench from each end.

Throwaway, until `iiac-perf analyze` can: it hard-codes the 10-50 trim and the `LSC trimmed` of
src/series.rs for ten runs.
"""

import json
import math
import statistics as st
import sys
from collections import defaultdict


def load(path):
    runs = defaultdict(list)
    for line in open(path):
        try:
            r = json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            continue
        runs[r["bench"]].append(r["mean_ns"])
    return {b: v for b, v in runs.items() if len(v) == 10}


def claim_pct(means):
    """`LSC trimmed` over the trimmed mean, in percent."""
    s = sorted(means)
    trimmed = sum(s[1:5]) / 4
    w = [min(max(m, s[1]), s[4]) for m in means]
    lsc = 2.447 * st.stdev(w) / (0.4 * math.sqrt(10)) * math.sqrt(2)
    return lsc / trimmed * 100


def main(paths, key):
    sessions = [load(p) for p in paths]
    rows = []
    for bench in sessions[0]:
        pcts = [claim_pct(s[bench]) for s in sessions if bench in s]
        rows.append((st.mean(pcts), max(pcts), bench, pcts))
    rows.sort(key=lambda r: r[1] if key == "worst" else r[0])
    print(f"{'rank':>4}  {'bench':18}{'LSC% mean':>10}{'worst':>8}   per session")
    for i, (mean, worst, bench, pcts) in enumerate(rows, 1):
        each = " ".join(f"{p:.3f}" for p in pcts)
        print(f"{i:4}  {bench:18}{mean:10.3f}{worst:8.3f}   {each}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    args = [a for a in sys.argv[1:] if not a.startswith("--")]
    if not args:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    main(args, "worst" if "--sort" in sys.argv and "worst" in sys.argv else "mean")

cd ../iiac-perf-expr-1/pins && python3 - <<'EOF'
p='README.md'; s=open(p).read()
anchor='## 3900X, 2026-09-19\n'
assert s.count(anchor)==1
note='''## Choosing the benches

Few benches and many invocations, where `../smooth/` is every bench and few sessions: this
experiment asks which measurement setup is trustworthy, and that one every bench, which the
other answers about thirty times cheaper per bench.

- Two, not one. One bench cannot show that the answer depends on the bench, and it does: on the
  7600X's `smt`, clock pinned, `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` claimed 0.185% and `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` 2.105%,
  eleven times wider, under the same settings on the same pair. Either alone would have said
  something true of itself and wrong of the setup. On the 3900X's `ccx` the same pair broke its
  claim 7 times in 28 and 0 times in 28.
- Not ten. The step from one to two buys the existence of that dependence; further benches buy
  its distribution, which `smooth` already has. The cost is linear and the harm worse: at ten
  benches the 7600X's 80 invocations would run about five hours instead of 54 minutes, and a
  session that long holds more of the drift the round-robin exists to spread.
- Pick them from the host's own `smooth` ranking, one narrow and one wide, and re-check per
  host. This pair brackets on the 7600X and does not on the 3900X, where `python3 rank.py`
  puts them 20th and 22nd of 28, both wide, claiming 0.80% and 1.08% where the pins sessions
  read 0.82% and 0.72%. So the bracket is a property of a host and a pair together, never of
  the pair, and inheriting one silently loses it. A 3900X pair chosen this way would be
  `zcr-mpsc-v0-2t` at 0.077% or `zcr-spsc-v2-2t` at 0.100% against `mpsc-2t` at 5.3%.
- The pair here is the two rings being optimized, which is a different reason for choosing them
  and the reason they were kept.

'''
open(p,'w').write(s.replace(anchor,note+anchor,1))
EOF

Note added, and the check you asked for says my "luck" line was too kind to itself. The bracketing is a 7600X property, not a property of the pair.

## The bracket does not hold on the 3900X

I ranked all 28 smooth benches by the width of the claim each makes about itself, as a percent of its own mean. The two pins benches land 20th and 22nd of 28:

| | 7600X `smt` | 3900X `smt` |
|---|---:|---:|
| `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` | 0.185% | 0.72% |
| `zcr-spsc-v3-2t` | 2.105% | 0.82% |
| ratio | 11x apart | 1.1x apart |

On the 3900X they're not a bracket at all: they're two adjacent benches, both in the wide third. So the pair doesn't bracket, a host and a pair together do, and inheriting a pair silently loses the property. That's worse than "luck" — it means the choice has to be remade per host.

A deliberately chosen 3900X pair would be `zcr-mpsc-v0-2t` at 0.077%, or `zcr-spsc-v2-2t` at 0.100%, against `mpsc-2t` at 5.3%.

The ranking is also a finding in its own right. Under one config, the benches span three orders of magnitude, from `cb-chan-1t` at 0.019% to `zcr-spsc-v3-1t` at 10.7%. Among the two-thread rings alone it's 0.077% to 5.3%. So "quick and trustworthy" is a property of a config *and a bench*, never of a config alone. That bears directly on what `iiac-perf.toml` can promise.

I kept the check as `smooth/rank.py` and wrote the finding into both READMEs. The pins note says two not one with the evidence, not ten with the reasons, and pick from the host's own ranking with this pair named as the counter-example.

## The XDG config

There is no `config.toml` yet. `~/.config/iiac-perf/` still holds only `config.md`, with `[freq]` and no `[profiles]`. Nothing has been installed.

And yes — only those two tables. That's the rule already in the cycle's deliberation, and I've now made the built files show it. They were 60 lines of commented-out template around two live tables, which invites exactly the leak we're trying to stop. They're now 30 and 26 lines: a header saying only `[freq]` and `[profiles]` belong here and why, then the two tables with their topology explained. Both parse, and `--pin-cpus smt` resolves to `11, 23` through the 3900X one.

To install:

```
cp tmp/xdg-3900x/iiac-perf/config.toml ~/.config/iiac-perf/config.toml
mv ~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md ~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md.bak
```

Both files present is a hard error, so the move matters. On the 7600X, the same with its file.

`vc-x1 validate --fast` passes. The rung is unchanged and still at its work review.
